\section{Estimate a reliable mapping}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/estimation:estimate-a-reliable-mapping}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/estimation:lec02-estimation}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/estimation::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Four matches can determine a homography, but real matches are noisy and some are wrong. \sphinxstylestrong{DLT} solves for the matrix; \sphinxstylestrong{RANSAC} finds matches that agree with one matrix. They solve different problems.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Source:} PDF pages 82–104, printed slides 83–105. These sections credit R. Hartley, A. Zisserman, and M. Pollefeys. {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/index::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{Lecture 3}}}} adds the assigned homography/probability quizzes and a full projective numerical walkthrough.


\subsection{DLT: turn matches into linear equations}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/estimation:dlt-turn-matches-into-linear-equations}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{direct linear transformation (DLT)} starts from \(x'\sim Hx\). Their cross product is zero because the vectors represent the same projective point: \(x'\times Hx=0\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For finite matches \((u,v)\leftrightarrow(u',v')\), multiply out the denominators in \eqref{equation:lectures/lecture02/homographies:eq-lec02-homography}. Each match supplies two independent equations in the nine entries of \(H\).

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — homography DLT system}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture02/estimation:eq-lec02-dlt}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
A_i&=\begin{pmatrix}
u&v&1&0&0&0&-u'u&-u'v&-u'\\
0&0&0&u&v&1&-v'u&-v'v&-v'
\end{pmatrix},\\
h&=(h_{11},h_{12},h_{13},h_{21},h_{22},h_{23},h_{31},h_{32},h_{33})^T,\\
A&=\begin{pmatrix}A_1\\\vdots\\A_n\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\min_{\|h\|=1}\|Ah\|^2.
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(A\) is \(2n\times9\), \(h\) is \(9\times1\). The constraint excludes the useless zero solution. Four nondegenerate exact matches give rank eight and a one\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional nullspace; with noisy extra matches, minimize the residual instead of expecting exact zero.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The finite\sphinxhyphen{}coordinate rows assume each destination’s last coordinate is nonzero. For ideal points, retain appropriate independent rows of the full cross\sphinxhyphen{}product system. Three cross\sphinxhyphen{}product equations have only two independent constraints; dropping the same row blindly can lose information.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Estimate a homography with SVD}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Normalize coordinates as described below; reject a degenerate four\sphinxhyphen{}point sample.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Stack two rows per match to form \(A\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \(A=U\Sigma V^T\) using singular value decomposition. Choose the \sphinxstylestrong{right singular vector} with smallest singular value and reshape it row by row into \(H\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Undo coordinate normalization and check projected matches.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For an \(8\times9\) system, request the full right\sphinxhyphen{}singular\sphinxhyphen{}vector basis: a reduced SVD can omit the ninth vector containing the nullspace. Do not confuse the last row of \(V^T\) with the last column of \(V^T\).

\end{TextbookBox}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Fixing \(h_{33}=1\) is a tempting shortcut, but valid homographies can have \(h_{33}=0\). Unit\sphinxhyphen{}vector normalization avoids privileging that entry. DLT minimizes \sphinxstylestrong{algebraic error}, which depends on coordinate scaling. Pixel reprojection error is a more interpretable final accuracy measure.

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/estimation:ex-lec02-dlt}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Worked example 2.4 — recover a simple planar map}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Source:} original numerical companion to PDF pages 83–94.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Match \((0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)\) to \((2,1),(4,1),(4,4),(2,4)\) in that order. The first correspondence produces rows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
(0,0,1,0,0,0,0,0,-2),\qquad
(0,0,0,0,0,1,0,0,-1).
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For \((1,0)\leftrightarrow(4,1)\) the rows are
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
(1,0,1,0,0,0,-4,0,-4),\qquad
(0,0,0,1,0,1,-1,0,-1).
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The other two matches fill the remaining four rows. The resulting matrix has rank eight. Its null vector, reshaped and rescaled, gives
\(H=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&2\\0&3&1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Check the unmeasured center: \(H(1/2,1/2,1)^T=(3,5/2,1)^T\), the center of the destination rectangle. All four measured corners reproject exactly. Three collinear source points would invalidate this four\sphinxhyphen{}point recovery.

\end{TextbookBox}


\subsection{Normalize: put the coordinates on a sensible scale}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/estimation:normalize-put-the-coordinates-on-a-sensible-scale}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Raw pixel coordinates may be hundreds, while their products in \(A\) reach tens of thousands. \sphinxstylestrong{Normalized DLT} recenters and rescales each image’s points independently, reducing this imbalance.

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — coordinate normalization and recovery}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture02/estimation:eq-lec02-normalize}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
c&=\frac1n\sum_i p_i,\quad
\bar r=\frac1n\sum_i\|p_i-c\|,\quad s=\frac{\sqrt2}{\bar r},\\
T&=\begin{pmatrix}s&0&-sc_u\\0&s&-sc_v\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\widetilde x=Tx,\quad \widetilde x'=T'x',\\
H&=(T')^{-1}\widetilde H T.
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(p_i=(u_i,v_i)^T\) are finite 2D points; \(T,T',H\) are \(3\times3\). The mean distance from the normalized centroid becomes \(\sqrt2\). Require \(\bar r>0\); coincident points provide no spatial information. Normalization improves conditioning, not incorrect matches or degeneracy.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Use normalized DLT}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute separate \(T,T'\) from the source and destination matches.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Fit \(\widetilde H\) to their normalized coordinates using \eqref{equation:lectures/lecture02/estimation:eq-lec02-dlt}.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Recover \(H=(T')^{-1}\widetilde H T\) and evaluate error in original coordinates.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The source square in Example 2.4 has centroid \((1/2,1/2)\), mean radius \(1/\sqrt2\), and scale \(s=2\). Its normalized corners are \((\pm1,\pm1)\), at radius \(\sqrt2\).

\end{TextbookBox}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Why this recovery order? The normalized mapping is \(T'x'\sim\widetilde H Tx\). Multiply by \((T')^{-1}\) to isolate the original destination coordinates. PDF page 92 also shows a simpler image\sphinxhyphen{}size scaling; it is an alternative heuristic, not the same transformation as centroid/mean\sphinxhyphen{}distance normalization.


\subsection{RANSAC: do not let wrong matches vote as measurements}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/estimation:ransac-do-not-let-wrong-matches-vote-as-measurements}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
An \sphinxstylestrong{{\hyperref[\detokenize{reference/glossary:term-Inlier}]{\sphinxtermref{\DUrole{xref,std,std-term}{inlier}}}}} agrees with the model within a chosen error threshold. An \sphinxstylestrong{outlier} does not. \sphinxstylestrong{{\hyperref[\detokenize{reference/glossary:term-RANSAC}]{\sphinxtermref{\DUrole{xref,std,std-term}{RANSAC}}}}} means random sample consensus: fit small random subsets, then count how many matches support each hypothesis.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.850\linewidth]{{ransac}.pdf}
\caption{The idea behind the lecture’s robust\sphinxhyphen{}line example: a large consistent group supports the correct model despite scattered bad measurements. Original schematic; homography hypotheses use four matches rather than two line points.}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/estimation:fig-lec02-ransac}}\end{figure}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — RANSAC trial count and inlier score}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture02/estimation:eq-lec02-ransac}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
N&=\left\lceil\frac{\log(1-p)}{\log(1-w^s)}\right\rceil,\\
r_i&=\|p_i'-\operatorname{dehom}(Hx_i)\|_2,\qquad
n_{\rm in}=\#\{i:r_i<\tau\}.
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(p\) is the desired probability of at least one all\sphinxhyphen{}inlier sample, \(w=1-e\) the inlier fraction, and \(s\) the sample size (four for a homography). Here residuals and threshold \(\tau\) are in destination pixels. \(N\) is a dimensionless integer.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The usual \(w^s\) model assumes independent draws, or a large pool approximating them, and nondegenerate all\sphinxhyphen{}inlier samples. Trials are independent. For sampling \(s\) distinct matches from a small pool of \(n\) containing \(I\) true inliers, the exact all\sphinxhyphen{}inlier probability is \(\binom I s/\binom n s\). Neither probability guarantees the selected model is correct.

\end{TextbookBox}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The derivation is short: a trial is all\sphinxhyphen{}inlier with probability \(w^s\). All \(N\) trials fail with probability \((1-w^s)^N\). Set that failure probability at most \(1-p\), take logarithms, and round up.

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Fit a homography robustly}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Sample four matches; reject collinear or otherwise degenerate configurations; estimate \(H\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Score every match against \(H\) using a fixed error definition and threshold.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Keep the best consensus and repeat to the trial budget. Update the budget from a better observed inlier ratio, while recognizing that it is an estimate.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Refit to the best inliers, then refine pixel reprojection error if needed.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \(w=0\) no finite budget succeeds; for \(w=1\) one nondegenerate trial suffices. A large consensus of repeated patterns can still support the wrong alignment. See Example 2.5.

\end{TextbookBox}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/estimation:ex-lec02-ransac}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Worked example 2.5 — why a better inlier fraction saves work}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Source:} numerical expansion of PDF page 98’s trial table; application figures from PDF page 104.

\sphinxAtStartPar
With \(p=0.99\), \(w=0.5\), and \(s=4\), the continuous budget is \(\log(0.01)/\log(15/16)\approx71.36\). Round \sphinxstylestrong{up} to 72 trials. At \(w=0.8\), it falls to 9.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The lecture’s building\sphinxhyphen{}image example starts with 268 putative matches. A 151\sphinxhyphen{}match consensus corresponds to roughly 56\% inliers; using that rounded ratio gives about 45 trials. The slide reports 43 iterations: the simple probability model is a budget estimate, not a reproduction of the implementation’s exact stopping history. Guided matching later finds 262 final inliers; this is a new matching stage, not simply the original consensus.

\end{TextbookBox}

\sphinxAtStartPar
An expected consensus threshold is approximately \(wn\) (rounded as needed), but it is not a statistical guarantee. \sphinxstylestrong{LMedS}, least median of squares, instead minimizes median squared residual; it is a different robust objective. Ordinary least squares can be dominated by gross outliers. Iterative refinement is useful \sphinxstylestrong{after} robust selection; iteration alone does not make an estimator robust.


\subsection{The complete slide pipeline}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/estimation:the-complete-slide-pipeline}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Detect interest points → propose matches → robustly estimate \(H\) → refine using inliers → use \(H\) to guide more matches. The slides name sum of absolute differences (SAD), sum of squared differences (SSD), and zero\sphinxhyphen{}mean normalized cross\sphinxhyphen{}correlation (ZNCC) as patch comparisons. SAD/SSD compare pixel intensities directly; ZNCC compares mean\sphinxhyphen{}centered, normalized patterns and needs nonzero patch variance. Lecture 5 develops matching and exposure changes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When motion is known to be small, restrict candidate locations; do not impose that restriction on arbitrary viewpoint changes. Nonlinear refinement may use Levenberg–Marquardt to minimize an image\sphinxhyphen{}error objective, rather than the initial algebraic DLT objective.

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Check 2.3 — can more points rescue a bad model?}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
Would fitting one homography to hundreds of matches on several depths always work better than using four floor corners?

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Answer}

\sphinxAtStartPar
No. Extra measurements cannot repair the wrong geometric model. With translation, a single homography generally fits one plane, not objects at many depths.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\section{Distortion and two\sphinxhyphen{}view geometry}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/two-view:distortion-and-two-view-geometry}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/two-view:lec02-two-view}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/two-view::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A planar warp is powerful, but it cannot explain curved lens distortion or general 3D parallax. The final slides introduce the tools for those cases.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Source:} PDF pages 105–129, printed slides 106–130; the section credits R. Hartley, A. Zisserman, and M. Pollefeys. The assigned epipolar/stereo quizzes and a fuller estimation treatment belong to Lecture 4.


\subsection{Straight lines first: correct lens distortion}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/two-view:straight-lines-first-correct-lens-distortion}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{{\hyperref[\detokenize{reference/glossary:term-Radial-distortion}]{\sphinxtermref{\DUrole{xref,std,std-term}{Radial distortion}}}}} moves points along directions from a distortion center. Straight scene edges can become curved. A homography preserves lines, so it cannot generally undo this bending.

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — radial correction model}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture02/two-view:eq-lec02-radial}
\begin{split}r^2=(u-c_u)^2+(v-c_v)^2,\quad
\begin{pmatrix}\widehat u\\\widehat v\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}c_u\\c_v\end{pmatrix}
+(1+k_1r^2+k_2r^4+\cdots)
\begin{pmatrix}u-c_u\\v-c_v\end{pmatrix}.\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here \((u,v)\) are measured distorted coordinates and hats denote corrected coordinates. The coefficients belong to \sphinxstylestrong{this correction direction}; a forward\sphinxhyphen{}distortion model generally needs different coefficients or numerical inversion. Use calibrated units: if \(r\) is in pixels, \(k_1\) has units pixel\(^{-2}\) and \(k_2\) pixel\(^{-4}\); normalized coordinates are also common.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This low\sphinxhyphen{}order model describes radial effects, not every lens defect. The distortion center may differ from the principal point. PDF page 109 mixes radius and squared\sphinxhyphen{}radius notation; writing \(r^2\) explicitly avoids that ambiguity.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Correct a point before geometric estimation}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the calibrated center, units, coefficients, and mapping direction.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \(r^2\) and the radial factor, then correct the coordinate.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check that straight scene edges become straighter; resample images with an appropriate inverse map.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For center \((0,0)\), point \((100,0)\) pixels, \(k_1=10^{-6}\) pixel\(^{-2}\), and no higher terms, the factor is \(1.01\) and the corrected point is \((101,0)\). A positive coefficient here expands radii; never transfer that sign interpretation to the inverse convention blindly.

\end{TextbookBox}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The slides suggest estimating distortion jointly with other camera parameters or by straightening known straight edges. Their room\sphinxhyphen{}image before/after sequence illustrates why this matters: ideal projective geometry should be applied to undistorted coordinates.


\subsection{One point becomes a line in the other image}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/two-view:one-point-becomes-a-line-in-the-other-image}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
With two camera centers \(C,C'\) and a scene point \(X\), the three define an \sphinxstylestrong{epipolar plane}. It cuts each image plane in an \sphinxstylestrong{{\hyperref[\detokenize{reference/glossary:term-Epipolar-line}]{\sphinxtermref{\DUrole{xref,std,std-term}{epipolar line}}}}}. If the first image point is known but its depth is not, its possible matches lie along that line in the second image.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{{\hyperref[\detokenize{reference/glossary:term-Epipole}]{\sphinxtermref{\DUrole{xref,std,std-term}{epipole}}}}} is the image of the other camera center; every epipolar line in an image passes through its epipole. The line between camera centers is the \sphinxstylestrong{baseline}.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[width=1.000\linewidth]{{epipolar}.pdf}
\caption{A special, rectified case: the right match must lie on the corresponding row. Its location along that row still depends on depth. Original schematic developing PDF pages 113–119.}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/two-view:fig-lec02-epipolar}}\end{figure}


\subsection{The fundamental matrix maps points to lines}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/two-view:the-fundamental-matrix-maps-points-to-lines}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — epipolar constraint and epipoles}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture02/two-view:eq-lec02-fundamental}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\ell'&=Fx,\qquad \ell=F^Tx',\qquad x'^TFx=0,\\
Fe&=0,\qquad F^Te'=0,\qquad \operatorname{rank}F=2.
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(x,x'\) are homogeneous image \(3\times1\) points; \(\ell,\ell'\) are line coefficients, \(e,e'\) epipoles. \(F\) is a \(3\times3\) \sphinxstylestrong{{\hyperref[\detokenize{reference/glossary:term-Fundamental-matrix}]{\sphinxtermref{\DUrole{xref,std,std-term}{fundamental matrix}}}}}, defined up to nonzero scale. It has seven DOF: nine entries minus scale minus the rank\sphinxhyphen{}two constraint. Reversing the image order transposes \(F\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
This ideal constraint assumes corresponding undistorted points and distinct camera centers. At an epipole, the corresponding line vector can vanish. Pure rotation has no nonzero baseline and does not determine a nonzero fundamental matrix from the camera pair. The equation constrains correspondence; it does not identify a unique match.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Turn a point into a correspondence constraint}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Multiply \(F\) by the first image point to obtain the second image’s line.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Test a candidate match by its dot product with that line.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For noisy data, use a scale\sphinxhyphen{}normalized geometric error instead of comparing raw \(x'^TFx\) values across arbitrary scalings.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Check matrix rank and image order. See Example 2.6.

\end{TextbookBox}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/two-view:ex-lec02-fundamental}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Worked example 2.6 — a horizontal epipolar line}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Source:} original numerical companion to the parallel\sphinxhyphen{}camera example, PDF page 119.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(F=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\0&0&-1\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(x=(2,3,1)^T\). Then \(Fx=(0,-1,3)^T\): candidate matches satisfy \(-v'+3=0\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Both \((5,3,1)^T\) and \((8,3,1)^T\) satisfy the constraint; \((5,4,1)^T\) does not. The two valid candidates show why an epipolar line is not a point prediction. The matrix has rank two and both epipoles are \((1,0,0)^T\), the horizontal ideal direction.

\end{TextbookBox}


\subsection{Where does the matrix come from?}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/two-view:where-does-the-matrix-come-from}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The source derives \(F\) by projecting two points on the first camera’s viewing ray into the second image. Their join is the epipolar line.

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — construct F from two camera matrices}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture02/two-view:eq-lec02-fcamera}
\begin{split}PC=0,\qquad e'=P'C,\qquad
F=[e']_\times P'P^+.\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(P,P'\) are rank\sphinxhyphen{}three \(3\times4\) camera matrices; \(C\) is the first camera center as a homogeneous 4\sphinxhyphen{}vector; \(P^+\) is a \(4\times3\) right pseudoinverse with \(PP^+=I_3\). The matrix \([e']_\times\) takes a cross product with \(e'\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For distinct centers, \(P^+x\) is one 3D point projecting to \(x\); adding \(\lambda C\) stays on its projective ray. Its second image lies on the line joining \(P'P^+x\) to \(P'C\), producing the formula. Coincident centers give \(P'C=0\), so this construction gives zero, not a valid rank\sphinxhyphen{}two \(F\).

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Check a camera\sphinxhyphen{}derived epipolar geometry}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Find a nonzero null vector \(C\) of \(P\) and compute \(e'=P'C\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Form the pseudoinverse and cross\sphinxhyphen{}product matrix, then multiply in the stated order.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Project a test 3D point in both cameras and verify the scalar constraint.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The cameras \(P=[I\mid0]\), \(P'=[I\mid(-1,0,0)^T]\) give Example 2.6’s matrix up to sign. A scene point \((2,3,1,1)^T\) projects to \((2,3,1)^T\) and \((1,3,1)^T\), on the same row.

\end{TextbookBox}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a fixed nondegenerate camera pair, \(F\) is unique \sphinxstylestrong{up to scale}. Estimating it from a finite set of matches can be ambiguous, particularly with planar scene points.

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — linear equations for F from matches}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture02/two-view:eq-lec02-eightpoint}
\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix}u'u&u'v&u'&v'u&v'v&v'&u&v&1\end{pmatrix}f=0,
\qquad Af=0.\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(f=(F_{11},F_{12},F_{13},F_{21},\ldots,F_{33})^T\) is \(9\times1\); one finite match contributes one row. At least eight suitably independent matches give the linear estimate. This differs from homography DLT’s \sphinxstylestrong{two} equations per match. Noisy linear solutions need a rank\sphinxhyphen{}two correction.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Recognize the eight\sphinxhyphen{}point estimation route}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Normalize both sets of image coordinates and stack the rows.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Find the smallest right singular vector and reshape it into a matrix.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Enforce rank two by setting its smallest singular value to zero.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Undo normalization: if normalized points are \(Tx,T'x'\), then \(F=T'^T\widetilde F T\); verify on held\sphinxhyphen{}out matches.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For Example 2.6 and match \((u,v)=(2,3)\), \((u',v')=(5,3)\), the row is \((10,15,5,6,9,3,2,3,1)\). Dotting it with the row\sphinxhyphen{}stacked \(F\) gives \(-3+3=0\). {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/estimation::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{Lecture 4}}}} develops noisy estimation and the assigned quiz calculations.

\end{TextbookBox}


\subsection{Motion patterns and rectification}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/two-view:motion-patterns-and-rectification}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The three slide examples show different locations for the epipoles:
\begin{itemize}
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Converging cameras:} epipolar lines fan toward finite epipoles, possibly outside the images.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Translation parallel to the image plane:} epipoles are ideal; for a horizontal baseline and aligned cameras, epipolar lines are horizontal.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Forward translation:} epipoles can lie inside the images, with radial epipolar lines. Ordinary rectangular planar rectification becomes problematic near that epipole.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{{\hyperref[\detokenize{reference/glossary:term-Rectification}]{\sphinxtermref{\DUrole{xref,std,std-term}{Rectification}}}}} warps two views so corresponding epipolar lines become matching horizontal rows. It simplifies the search from two dimensions to one; it does not eliminate matching ambiguity or depth variation.

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — rectified coordinates and line geometry}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture02/two-view:eq-lec02-rectify}
\begin{split}\bar x\sim Hx,\quad \bar x'\sim H'x',\quad
\bar F=H'^{-T}FH^{-1},\qquad
He\sim H'e'\sim(1,0,0)^T.\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(H,H'\) are nonsingular \(3\times3\) image warps. Moving both epipoles to the horizontal ideal point makes epipolar lines horizontal; the two warps must also align the corresponding row coordinates. A finite epipole is sent to infinity, so its neighborhood cannot retain a finite undistorted rectangular image.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Interpret a rectified pair}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Estimate camera/epipolar geometry and choose compatible rectifying warps.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Resample both images by inverse warping.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check that known matches share the same row; then search along that row.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Example 2.6 is already rectified: identity warps preserve its horizontal lines and equal\sphinxhyphen{}row constraint. The final slide’s paired objects illustrate the visual goal. {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{Stereo depth and error}}}} follow in Lecture 4.

\end{TextbookBox}

\subsection{Spring 2020 Quiz 1 — Projective points and camera projection}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/quiz-workbook:spring-2020-quiz-1-projective-points-and-camera-projection}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/quiz-workbook:quiz-source-8}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Historical source:} \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{3dcvMid/olderquizzes/cs532s20\_quiz1.pdf}}.


\subsubsection{Problem 1}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/quiz-workbook:problem-1}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/quiz-workbook:quiz-8-q1}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/quiz-workbook:ex-lec02-collinear}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original problem · quiz booklet}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
For projective\sphinxhyphen{}plane points \(a,b,c\), use only dot and cross products to test whether they are collinear. In what case does the test fail?

\par\medskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Fully worked solution} — red labels explain the step; blue mathematics shows the calculation.

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Join two projective points}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The cross product constructs their homogeneous line.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Recall that the homogeneous \sphinxstyleemphasis{line through two distinct points} is their cross product: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\ell=a\times b\)}.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Test the third point}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} A point is on a line exactly when their dot product is zero.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A third point {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(c\)} lies on {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\ell\)} exactly when its dot product with {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\ell\)} is zero. Thus test {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\boxed{c^T(a\times b)=0}\)}. This equals the determinant of the matrix with columns {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(a,b,c\)}.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 3 — Handle repeated points}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} A zero cross product cannot identify a unique joining line.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(a\sim b\)}, then {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(a\times b=0\)}, so it does not construct a unique line. Choose a distinct pair instead. The determinant still correctly says the three representatives are linearly dependent: any repeated point together with a third point lies on at least one line. A zero homogeneous point itself is invalid.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 4 — Expand a numerical test}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Actual products show both a passing and a failing candidate.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Original numerical companion: take {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(a=(0,0,1)^T\)}, {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(b=(2,0,1)^T\)}, {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(c=(5,0,1)^T\)}. Then
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
a\times b=\begin{pmatrix}0(1)-1(0)\\1(2)-0(1)\\0(0)-0(2)\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
c^T(a\times b)=\begin{pmatrix}5&0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\0\end{pmatrix}=0.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The points lie on {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(Y=0\)}. Replacing {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(c\)} by {\color{QuizMathBlue} \((5,1,1)^T\)} gives {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(5(0)+1(2)+1(0)=2\)}, so that point is off the line.

\par


\subsubsection{Problem 2(a–b)}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/quiz-workbook:problem-2-ab}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/quiz-workbook:quiz-8-q2}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/quiz-workbook:ex-lec02-projection}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original problem · quiz booklet}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(X=(X,Y,Z,W)^T\) be a homogeneous 3D point and \(x\sim MX\) a homogeneous 2D image point. Find (a) the dimensions of \(M\); (b) explicit inhomogeneous image coordinates from the entries \(m_{ij}\) and \(X\).

\par\medskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Fully worked solution} — red labels explain the step; blue mathematics shows the calculation.

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Count input and output entries}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Matrix multiplication determines the camera matrix’s dimensions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A 3D homogeneous point has four components; a 2D homogeneous image point has three. Therefore {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\boxed{M\in\mathbb R^{3\times4}}\)} and {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(Mx\!\)} is \sphinxstyleemphasis{not} the mapping; the correct product is {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(MX\in\mathbb R^{3\times1}\)}.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Multiply the full projection matrix}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Every output entry is one row dotted with the world point.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Show the full matrix\sphinxhyphen{}vector product:
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\begin{aligned}
q&=\begin{pmatrix}m_{11}&m_{12}&m_{13}&m_{14}\\m_{21}&m_{22}&m_{23}&m_{24}\\m_{31}&m_{32}&m_{33}&m_{34}\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}X\\Y\\Z\\W\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\begin{pmatrix}m_{11}X+m_{12}Y+m_{13}Z+m_{14}W\\m_{21}X+m_{22}Y+m_{23}Z+m_{24}W\\m_{31}X+m_{32}Y+m_{33}Z+m_{34}W\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 3 — Divide by the last coordinate}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Homogeneous image coordinates represent ratios.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A finite homogeneous point represents ratios, so divide the first two entries by the third:
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\begin{aligned}
u&=\frac{m_{11}X+m_{12}Y+m_{13}Z+m_{14}W}{m_{31}X+m_{32}Y+m_{33}Z+m_{34}W},\\
v&=\frac{m_{21}X+m_{22}Y+m_{23}Z+m_{24}W}{m_{31}X+m_{32}Y+m_{33}Z+m_{34}W}.
\end{aligned}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For a finite world point choose {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(W=1\)}. If {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(q_3=0\)} and {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(q\ne0\)}, the result is an ideal image point; if {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(q=0\)}, projection is undefined.

\par


\subsubsection{Problem 3(a–b)}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/quiz-workbook:problem-3-ab}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/quiz-workbook:quiz-8-q3}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/quiz-workbook:ex-lec02-intersections}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original problem · quiz booklet}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(\ell_1,\ell_2\) be two distinct vertical lines each at distance \(d>0\) from the 2D origin, and \(\ell_3\) the horizontal line through the origin. Give their homogeneous line vectors and count the possible pairwise intersections.

\par\medskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Fully worked solution} — red labels explain the step; blue mathematics shows the calculation.

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Represent the vertical lines}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Their equations fix the signs of the constant coefficients.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Choose {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\ell_1:x=d\)} and {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\ell_2:x=-d\)}; as {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(ax+by+c=0\)}, their vectors are {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\boxed{\ell_1=(1,0,-d)^T}\)}, {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\boxed{\ell_2=(1,0,d)^T}\)}.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Represent the horizontal line}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The line through the origin has no constant offset.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the horizontal line {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(y=0\)}, use {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\boxed{\ell_3=(0,1,0)^T}\)}. Line vectors are homogeneous, so nonzero multiples are equivalent.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 3 — Compute both finite intersections}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Cross products intersect homogeneous lines.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute both finite intersections component by component:
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\begin{aligned}
\ell_1\times\ell_3&=\begin{pmatrix}0(0)-(-d)(1)\\(-d)(0)-1(0)\\1(1)-0(0)\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}d\\0\\1\end{pmatrix},\\
\ell_2\times\ell_3&=\begin{pmatrix}0(0)-d(1)\\d(0)-1(0)\\1(1)-0(0)\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}-d\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Their final coordinates are already one, giving ordinary points {\color{QuizMathBlue} \((d,0)\)} and {\color{QuizMathBlue} \((-d,0)\)}.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 4 — Intersect the parallel lines}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} A zero last coordinate represents a point at infinity.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The parallel vertical lines give
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\ell_1\times\ell_2=\begin{pmatrix}0(d)-(-d)(0)\\(-d)(1)-1(d)\\1(0)-0(1)\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-2d\\0\end{pmatrix}\sim\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The last coordinate is zero, so do not divide: this is a point at infinity in the vertical direction.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 5 — Count in the stated geometry}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Projective and finite\sphinxhyphen{}plane intersection counts differ.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\boxed{3\text{ projective intersections}}\)} among the 3 line pairs, of which {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\boxed{2\text{ are finite}}\)}. Say both numbers to clarify the geometric convention.

\par

\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.700\linewidth]{{quiz-lines}.pdf}
\caption{Two finite intersections and one vertical point at infinity.}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/quiz-workbook:id1}}\end{figure}

\sphinxAtStartPar

Undo coordinate normalization in the correct order.

\section{TLDR}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/tldr:tldr}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/tldr:lec02-tldr}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/tldr::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Lecture 2 in one sentence:} estimate planar image mappings from trustworthy matches, resample them correctly, and recognize when distortion or 3D depth requires another model.


\subsection{The important things}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/tldr:the-important-things}}\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Convert quaternions consistently.} This chapter adds quaternion\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}matrix and matrix\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}quaternion formulas. The scalar extraction is \(w=\tfrac12\sqrt{1+\operatorname{tr}R}\); near a half\sphinxhyphen{}turn, use a largest\sphinxhyphen{}component branch. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/quaternions:lec02-quaternions}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Quaternions: convert without changing the rotation}}}}.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{SLERP interpolates orientations.} Align endpoint quaternion signs, then interpolate along the unit sphere. For nearly identical orientations, normalized linear interpolation avoids an unstable denominator.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{A plane can be rectified with four nondegenerate matches.} A homography supplies the mapping; the destination rectangle’s aspect ratio needs known geometry for metric accuracy. Raised objects and hidden floor cannot be reconstructed by a floor warp. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/homographies:lec02-homographies}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Homographies: straighten a photographed plane}}}}.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Cross\sphinxhyphen{}ratio survives perspective.} For four ordered collinear coordinates, \(\operatorname{CR}(a,b;c,d)=(c-a)(d-b)/((c-b)(d-a))\). Ordinary spacings may change while this value stays fixed.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Inverse warping fills the output grid.} For each destination pixel, use \(H^{-1}\) to locate its source sample. Bilinear interpolation blends four neighbors with weights summing to one; strong shrinking also needs antialiasing. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/warping:lec02-warping}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Image warping: where do the new pixels come from?}}}}.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{DLT estimates the mapping; normalization stabilizes it.} Each homography match contributes two rows to a \(2n\times9\) system. The smallest right singular vector supplies the matrix entries. Normalize each image independently, then recover \(H=(T')^{-1}\widetilde H T\). See {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/estimation:lec02-estimation}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Estimate a reliable mapping}}}}.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{RANSAC rejects inconsistent matches.} Sample → fit → score → repeat → refit. Under its sampling assumptions, use \(N=\lceil\log(1-p)/\log(1-w^s)\rceil\), where \(w\) is the inlier fraction, \(s\) the sample size, and \(p\) the desired sampling success probability. Consensus is not proof of a correct model.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Distortion and depth variation require different tools.} Radial correction straightens lens\sphinxhyphen{}bent edges. The fundamental matrix constrains correspondence by \(\ell'=Fx\) and \(x'^TFx=0\); it has rank two and seven DOF. Rectification aligns corresponding epipolar lines with matching rows. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/two-view:lec02-two-view}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Distortion and two\sphinxhyphen{}view geometry}}}}.

\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Question 1}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/tldr:question-1}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/tldr:lec02-tldr-q1}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original practice question}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a proper rotation with trace zero, what scalar quaternion component does the trace branch give?

\par\medskip

\par\medskip
\textbf{Worked solution}\par\smallskip

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Insert the trace}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} This branch extracts the nonnegative quaternion scalar from a proper rotation.
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
w=\frac12\sqrt{1+\operatorname{tr}R}=\frac12\sqrt{1+0}=\frac12.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — State the sign convention}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} A quaternion and its negative encode the same rotation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The trace branch chooses {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(w=+1/2\)}; negating the entire quaternion gives an equivalent representation.

\par

\par\medskip


\subsubsection{Question 2}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/tldr:question-2}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/tldr:lec02-tldr-q2}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original practice question}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
Before SLERP, what should you do if the endpoint quaternions have a negative dot product?

\par\medskip

\par\medskip
\textbf{Worked solution}\par\smallskip

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Inspect the quaternion dot product}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Opposite quaternion signs can describe equivalent rotations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(q_0^Tq_1<0\)}, replace one endpoint by its negative: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(q_1\leftarrow-q_1\)}.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Check the resulting path}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Sign alignment avoids taking the unnecessarily long interpolation arc.
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
q_0^T(-q_1)=-q_0^Tq_1>0.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
SLERP then uses sign\sphinxhyphen{}aligned endpoints for a shortest rotation path; handle nearly equal endpoints with a stable interpolation branch.

\par

\par\medskip


\subsubsection{Question 3}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/tldr:question-3}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/tldr:lec02-tldr-q3}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original practice question}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
What is \(\operatorname{CR}(0,1;2,3)\)? Should a projective warp of the line change it?

\par\medskip

\par\medskip
\textbf{Worked solution}\par\smallskip

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Substitute all four coordinates}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The ordering fixes which cross\sphinxhyphen{}ratio is being evaluated.
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\operatorname{CR}(0,1;2,3)=\frac{(2-0)(3-1)}{(2-1)(3-0)}=\frac{2\cdot2}{1\cdot3}=\frac43.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Apply projective invariance}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} A valid projectivity preserves this ordered collinear ratio.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The warped points have the same cross\sphinxhyphen{}ratio {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(4/3\)}, even when their ordinary distances change. Keep their order and handle ideal coordinates homogeneously if needed.

\par

\par\medskip


\subsubsection{Question 4}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/tldr:question-4}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/tldr:lec02-tldr-q4}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original practice question}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
How many nondegenerate matches and how many DLT rows are needed for a minimal homography estimate?

\par\medskip

\par\medskip
\textbf{Worked solution}\par\smallskip

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Count the constraints}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Each homography correspondence supplies two independent linear rows.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A homography has nine entries up to one common nonzero scale, leaving eight degrees of freedom. Four pairs give {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(2(4)=8\)} equations.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — State the system and its rank}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} A unique homogeneous solution needs a one\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional nullspace.
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
A\in\mathbb R^{8\times9},\qquad \operatorname{rank}A=8,\qquad Ah=0.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Four nondegenerate matches are minimal; degenerate arrangements need additional usable information.

\par

\par\medskip


\subsubsection{Question 5}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/tldr:question-5}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/tldr:lec02-tldr-q5}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original practice question}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
A source\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}destination warp translates content by \((6,-2)\) pixels. Where does destination pixel \((10,10)\) sample?

\par\medskip

\par\medskip
\textbf{Worked solution}\par\smallskip

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Invert the translation}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} An output pixel must look backward to its source location.
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
H^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&-6\\0&1&2\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Multiply the output pixel}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The inverse warp identifies which source pixel to sample.
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
H^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}10\\10\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}10-6\\10+2\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\12\\1\end{pmatrix}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Sample source {\color{QuizMathBlue} \((4,12)\)}.

\par

\par\medskip


\subsubsection{Question 6}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/tldr:question-6}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/tldr:lec02-tldr-q6}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original practice question}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
Four neighboring intensities are \(0,20,40,60\). What is their bilinear value at the center of the square?

\par\medskip

\par\medskip
\textbf{Worked solution}\par\smallskip

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Find the four weights}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The center is halfway along both axes of the square.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each bilinear weight is {\color{QuizMathBlue} \((1/2)(1/2)=1/4\)}. The weights sum to one.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Take the weighted sum}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Bilinear interpolation combines all four neighboring values.
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
I=\frac14(0)+\frac14(20)+\frac14(40)+\frac14(60)=\frac{120}{4}=30.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip


\subsubsection{Question 7}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/tldr:question-7}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/tldr:lec02-tldr-q7}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original practice question}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \(p=0.99\), \(w=0.8\), \(s=4\), is the standard RANSAC budget 8 or 9 trials? Does it guarantee the correct model?

\par\medskip

\par\medskip
\textbf{Worked solution}\par\smallskip

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Compute one clean\sphinxhyphen{}sample probability}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The standard model treats the four sampled inlier statuses as independent.
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
q=w^s=0.8^4=0.4096.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Round the trial budget upward}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} A fractional number of trials must be rounded up to meet the target probability.
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
N=\left\lceil\frac{\ln(1-0.99)}{\ln(1-0.4096)}\right\rceil=\lceil8.7392\ldots\rceil=9.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 3 — Interpret the guarantee correctly}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Sampling success alone cannot certify the final model.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The calculation concerns at least one clean sample under the stated assumptions. Degeneracy, an unsuitable threshold or ambiguous image content can still spoil the estimated model.

\par

\par\medskip


\subsubsection{Question 8}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/tldr:question-8}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/tldr:lec02-tldr-q8}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original practice question}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
If \(Fx=(0,-1,4)^T\), what must a matching ordinary point \((u',v')\) satisfy? Is \(u'\) determined?

\par\medskip

\par\medskip
\textbf{Worked solution}\par\smallskip

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Test point\sphinxhyphen{}line incidence}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The three supplied numbers are line coefficients.
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\begin{pmatrix}u'&v'&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0\\-1\\4\end{pmatrix}=0u'-v'+4=0.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Read the free coordinate}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} A line imposes one equation on two ordinary coordinates.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(v'=4\)}, while {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(u'\)} is not determined. Image evidence must select the actual match along the line.

\par

\par\medskip

\section{From field of view to a camera matrix}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/calibration:from-field-of-view-to-a-camera-matrix}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/calibration:lec03-calibration}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/calibration::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A wider view fits more of the scene into the same image. That means a shorter focal length \sphinxstylestrong{in pixels}. A right triangle tells us exactly how much shorter.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Sources:} lecture PDF pages 3–12; Spring 2019 Quiz 2, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cs532s19\_quiz2\sphinxhyphen{}2.pdf}}, P1–P4, PDF page 1. Spring 2020 Quiz 3, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cs532s20\_quiz3.pdf}}, page 1, repeats these questions under a mixed Spring 2019/Spring 2020 header.

\index{Field of view@\spxentry{Field of view}!Pixel pitch; Principal point@\spxentry{Pixel pitch; Principal point}}\ignorespaces

\subsection{Fit the view into the image}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/calibration:fit-the-view-into-the-image}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/calibration:index-0}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{horizontal field of view} \(\theta\) is the angle between the rays through the left and right image boundaries. For a centered, undistorted pinhole image, half the image width and the focal length form a right triangle.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.800\linewidth]{{fov}.pdf}
\caption{Half the view makes a right triangle: opposite side \(W/2\), adjacent side \(f_x\). Both lengths must use the same units.}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/calibration:fig-lec03-fov}}\end{figure}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — focal length from centered horizontal field of view}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture03/calibration:eq-lec03-fov}
\begin{split}\tan\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{W/2}{f_x},\qquad
f_x=\frac{W}{2\tan(\theta/2)}.\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(W\) is image width in pixels, \(f_x\) is horizontal focal length in pixels, and \(0<\theta<180^\circ\). Use a centered principal point and a rectilinear pinhole model. An off\sphinxhyphen{}center principal point needs separate left/right angles; strong lens distortion needs its own model.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Build a calibration estimate}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Input:} image width and horizontal FOV. Set the calculator’s angle units correctly.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \(f_x\) with the boxed equation.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To form \(K\), supply the remaining assumptions: vertical focal length, skew, and principal point.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Check:} doubling image resolution at unchanged FOV doubles focal length in pixels. A wider FOV reduces it.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
FOV alone does not determine every entry of \(K\).

\end{TextbookBox}

The \sphinxstylestrong{principal point} is where the optical axis meets the image plane. Its pixel coordinates, normalized coordinates, and physical 3D position describe related things in different units.

\section{Find depth when the point lies on a known plane}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/ray-plane:find-depth-when-the-point-lies-on-a-known-plane}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/ray-plane:lec03-ray-plane}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/ray-plane::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
One pixel supplies a ray, not a distance. A known plane supplies the missing condition: \sphinxstylestrong{keep moving along the ray until you reach the plane}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Sources:} lecture PDF pages 3–12; Spring 2020 Quiz 2, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cs532s20\_quiz2.pdf}}, P1–P2, PDF page 1; \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cs532f15\_quiz9.pdf}}, P1, PDF page 1, printed \sphinxstylestrong{Spring 2019 Quiz 9} despite the filename.


\subsection{First, keep the two kinds of coordinates straight}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/ray-plane:first-keep-the-two-kinds-of-coordinates-straight}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Worked example 3.3 — two points on one viewing ray.} {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/quiz-workbook:quiz-14-q1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Read the original problem and every worked step}}}}.


\subsection{Intersect the ray with a plane}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/ray-plane:intersect-the-ray-with-a-plane}}
\index{Ray–plane intersection@\spxentry{Ray–plane intersection}!Axial depth@\spxentry{Axial depth}}\ignorespaces
\sphinxAtStartPar
Suppose the known plane is \(AX+BY+CZ+D=0\). Here \(A,B,C\) are plane coefficients, not the point named \(A\) in the previous example. Work entirely in the \sphinxstylestrong{camera frame}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The image coordinate \((x',y')\) lies on a virtual plane at focal length \(f\). These three values use the same physical length unit. The ray direction with third component one is
\(q=(x'/f,y'/f,1)^T\). If you start with a pixel \((u,v)\) instead, first obtain \(q=K^{-1}(u,v,1)^T\) under the pinhole model; correct distortion before this step when necessary.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A scene point at axial depth \(Z\) is \(P=Zq\). Substitute its coordinates into the plane:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
A\frac{Zx'}f+B\frac{Zy'}f+CZ+D=0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
Z\left(A\frac{x'}f+B\frac{y'}f+C\right)=-D.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — depth from a ray and a plane}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture03/ray-plane:eq-lec03-ray-plane}
\begin{split}\gamma=(A,B,C)\,q,\qquad
Z=-\frac{D}{\gamma}
 =-\frac{Df}{Ax'+By'+Cf},\qquad P=Zq.\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Require \((A,B,C)\ne\mathbf0\) and \(\gamma\ne0\). \(Z\) is \sphinxstylestrong{axial depth}, not Euclidean range. For dimensionless normal coefficients and \(D\) in meters, \(Z\) is in meters. Rescaling the plane coefficients leaves the result unchanged.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Recover a 3D point on the known plane}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Input:} a calibrated image coordinate and plane coefficients in the camera frame.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Form \(q\) with third component one. Compute \(\gamma=(A,B,C)q\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If \(\gamma\ne0\), calculate \(Z=-D/\gamma\) and \(P=Zq\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Check:} substitute \(P\) into the plane and reproject it. For a point visible in front of this camera, require \(Z>0\).

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Near\sphinxhyphen{}parallel rays amplify input errors. Judge this using the angle between the ray and plane, rather than an unnormalized denominator.

\end{TextbookBox}

\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.850\linewidth]{{ray-plane}.pdf}
\caption{A side view of Example 3.4. The image\sphinxhyphen{}plane intersection fixes the ray; the scene\sphinxhyphen{}plane intersection fixes its depth. The \(Y\) coordinate is suppressed only in the drawing.}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/ray-plane:fig-lec03-ray-plane}}\end{figure}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/ray-plane:ex-lec03-plane}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Worked example 3.4 — put numbers into the depth answer}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Adapted from:} printed Spring 2019 Quiz 9, P1, whose requested symbolic answer is \eqref{equation:lectures/lecture03/ray-plane:eq-lec03-ray-plane}. The following numbers are an original companion.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Given:} plane \(X+Z=10\), \(f=2\), \((x',y')=(0.5,0.25)\), all lengths in the same unit.
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Plane coefficients: \((A,B,C,D)=(1,0,1,-10)\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Ray: \(q=(0.25,0.125,1)^T\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Denominator: \(\gamma=1(0.25)+0(0.125)+1=1.25\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Depth: \(Z=10/1.25=8\); point \(P=(2,1,8)^T\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check the plane: \(2+8=10\). Check projection: \((fX/Z,fY/Z)=(0.5,0.25)\).

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The point is eight units forward along the optical axis. Its distance from the camera is \(\sqrt{2^2+1^2+8^2}=\sqrt{69}\), a little larger.

\end{TextbookBox}

\section{Recover a genuinely projective homography}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/homography-practice:recover-a-genuinely-projective-homography}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/homography-practice:lec03-dlt-practice}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/homography-practice::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The earlier DLT example recovered a shifted, stretched rectangle. This one adds a \sphinxstylestrong{changing denominator}: a square becomes a trapezoid, and its center does not map to the average of the destination corners.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Source:} original numerical companion to lecture PDF pages 34–45, addressing the DLT/SVD priority in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ExamToDo.md}}. Use the canonical {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/estimation::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{DLT rows and SVD procedure}}}}; this section follows those steps with complete projective data.

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/homography-practice:ex-lec03-dlt}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Worked example 3.5 — normalize, solve, and recover}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Given:} the following four exact correspondences, in the same order.


\begin{savenotes}\sphinxattablestart
\sphinxthistablewithglobalstyle
\centering
\begin{tabulary}{\linewidth}[t]{TT}
\sphinxtoprule
\sphinxstyletheadfamily
\sphinxAtStartPar
Source \((u,v)\)
&\sphinxstyletheadfamily
\sphinxAtStartPar
Destination \((u',v')\)
\\
\sphinxmidrule
\sphinxtableatstartofbodyhook
\sphinxAtStartPar
\((0,0)\)
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
\((0,0)\)
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\((1,0)\)
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
\((2,0)\)
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\((1,1)\)
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
\((2,1)\)
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\((0,1)\)
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
\((0,2)\)
\\
\sphinxbottomrule
\end{tabulary}
\sphinxtableafterendhook\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{1. Normalize each image independently.} For the source square, centroid \((0.5,0.5)\) and mean radius \(1/\sqrt2\) give scale \(2\). For the destination, centroid \((1,0.75)\) and mean radius \(1.28288937\) give scale \(1.10236596\). Thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
T=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&-1\\0&2&-1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
T'\approx\begin{pmatrix}1.102366&0&-1.102366\\0&1.102366&-0.826774\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The destination mean radius is the average of \(1.25,1.25,\sqrt{1.0625},\sqrt{2.5625}\). This is \sphinxstylestrong{mean distance}, not root\sphinxhyphen{}mean\sphinxhyphen{}square distance.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{2. Fill the normalized DLT rows.} For the first pair,
\(\widetilde x=(-1,-1,1)^T\) and \(\widetilde x'\approx(-1.102366,-0.826774,1)^T\).
Its two rows, using \eqref{equation:lectures/lecture02/estimation:eq-lec02-dlt}, are approximately
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\begin{aligned}
(&-1,-1,1,0,0,0,-1.102366,-1.102366,1.102366),\\
(&0,0,0,-1,-1,1,-0.826774,-0.826774,0.826774).
\end{aligned}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The other three pairs supply six more rows. The stacked matrix \(\widetilde A\) is \(8\times9\) with rank eight.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{3. Read the full right null vector.} A full SVD returns a \(9\times9\) right\sphinxhyphen{}vector basis. One unit null vector, rounded here, is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
h\approx(0.627538,0,0.209179,-0.156884,0.418359,-0.052295,
0.189755,0,0.569265)^T.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Its negative is equally valid. Reshape \sphinxstylestrong{row by row}, then rescale for display so the last entry is one:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\widetilde H\approx\begin{pmatrix}
1.102366&0&0.367455\\
-0.275591&0.734911&-0.091864\\
1/3&0&1
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Request the full basis: the eight singular values returned for an \(8\times9\) matrix do not themselves include a ninth listed zero. The extra right vector supplies its exact nullspace.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{4. Undo normalization.} Apply \eqref{equation:lectures/lecture02/estimation:eq-lec02-normalize}, using unrounded numbers in the calculation:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
H=(T')^{-1}\widetilde H T
\ \sim\ \begin{pmatrix}4&0&0\\0&2&0\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{5. Check a corner and a point you did not fit.} For \((1,1)\), the homogeneous result is \((4,2,2)^T\), hence \((2,1)\): correct. The unmeasured square center gives
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
H(1/2,1/2,1)^T=(2,1,3/2)^T
\quad\Rightarrow\quad (u',v')=(4/3,2/3).
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
That differs from the destination vertex average \((1,3/4)\). Perspective does not preserve ordinary averages. The nonzero \(h_{31}\) makes the denominator depend on \(u\).

\end{TextbookBox}

\caption{The orange point is the mapped source center. The destination’s marked vertex average is elsewhere; averaging coordinates is not a projective operation.}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/homography-practice:fig-lec03-dlt}}\end{figure}

The {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture02/homographies::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{court\sphinxhyphen{}rectification example}}}} is the slide deck’s real\sphinxhyphen{}image application, repeated here on PDF page 22. Here the pool is unusually small. Four independent draws are an approximation to a real four\sphinxhyphen{}correspondence sampler. If asked for an \sphinxstylestrong{exact} count, specify the sampling rule.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Why the last denominator? Choose four of five source corners, four of five destination corners, then one of \(4!\) bijections: \(5\times5\times24=600\) valid sets. Only five are subsets of the intended five matches. These are different experiments, so their trial counts need not agree. If rejected draws consume runtime, include their cost separately.

\subsection{More trials cannot solve a symmetry}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture03/probability-ransac:more-trials-cannot-solve-a-symmetry}}
