\section{Stereo depth, sensitivity and worked error examples}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:stereo-depth-sensitivity-and-worked-error-examples}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:lec04-stereo}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Hold a finger in front of your face and close one eye at a time. Its apparent horizontal shift is larger when it is close. \sphinxstylestrong{Disparity} measures that shift in a rectified camera pair.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Quick route:} {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:stereo-derive-depth}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{derive depth}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:stereo-depth-sensitivity}]{\sphinxcrossref{understand sensitivity}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:ex-lec04-stereo-fall}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Fall quiz: ±1 pixel}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:ex-lec04-stereo-spring}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Spring quiz: larger errors}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:stereo-explorer}]{\sphinxcrossref{3D explorer}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:ex-lec04-search}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{depth range → search range}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Sources:} lecture PDF pages 58–64; Fall 2025 Quiz 3, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cs532f25\_quiz\_3\_solution.pdf}}, Q1–Q2, page 1; Spring 2019 Quiz 5, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cs532s19\_quiz5\sphinxhyphen{}2.pdf}}, P1’s three bullets, page 1; Spring 2020 Quiz 5, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cs532s20\_quiz5.pdf}}, same questions under an overprinted 2019/2020 header.

\index{Disparity@\spxentry{Disparity}}\ignorespaces
\index{Stereo depth@\spxentry{Stereo depth}}\ignorespaces
\index{Depth uncertainty@\spxentry{Depth uncertainty}}\ignorespaces

\subsection{Turn horizontal shift into axial depth}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:turn-horizontal-shift-into-axial-depth}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:stereo-derive-depth}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:index-2}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:index-0}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Assume aligned rectified cameras with a horizontal baseline \(b>0\), shared horizontal focal length \(f\) in pixels, and matched principal\sphinxhyphen{}point columns. Put the left center at \((0,0,0)\) and the right center at \((b,0,0)\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a scene point \((X,Y,Z)\), the left camera sees horizontal position \(X\), while the right camera sees \(X-b\) relative to its own center. Perspective divides each by the same depth:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}u_L-c_x=\frac{fX}{Z},\qquad u_R-c_x=\frac{f(X-b)}{Z}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Subtract the right observation from the left.} The principal point cancels, then the unknown \(X\) cancels:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\begin{aligned}
d&=(u_L-c_x)-(u_R-c_x)\\
&=\frac{fX}{Z}-\frac{f(X-b)}{Z}
=\frac{fX-fX+fb}{Z}=\frac{fb}{Z}.
\end{aligned}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Multiply both sides by \(Z\), giving \(dZ=fb\). Divide by positive \(d\): \sphinxstylestrong{\(Z=fb/d\)}. This is why the horizontal shift alone can recover depth once the cameras are calibrated.

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — rectified stereo depth}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture04/stereo:eq-lec04-depth}
\begin{split}d=u_L-u_R,\qquad Z=\frac{fb}{d}.\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(f\) and \(d\) use pixels; \(Z\) uses the same length unit as \(b\). \(Z\) is axial depth. Require \(d>0\) under this camera order and forward\sphinxhyphen{}view convention. If principal\sphinxhyphen{}point columns differ, use corrected disparity \(d=(u_L-c_{xL})-(u_R-c_{xR})\) instead. A zero disparity is the ideal infinite\sphinxhyphen{}depth limit, not a finite reconstruction.

\end{TextbookBox}

\Needspace{12\baselineskip}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Reconstruct with a known baseline}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Input:} rectified correspondence, calibrated pixel focal length, and baseline length.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check equal image rows and subtract horizontal coordinates in the stated order.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \(Z=fb/d\). Then use {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture01/cameras::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{calibrated backprojection}}}} if you also need \(X,Y\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Check:} doubling disparity halves depth; doubling baseline at fixed disparity doubles depth. Keep centimeters and meters consistent.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The source’s BAD/GOOD rectification examples (PDF pages 59–60) illustrate that stereo needs compatible row alignment, not independently straightened pictures.

\end{TextbookBox}

\subsection{Stereo depth sensitivity: why one pixel matters}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:stereo-depth-sensitivity-why-one-pixel-matters}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:stereo-depth-sensitivity}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Faraway points barely move between the two images.} Their disparity is small, so one pixel is a large fraction of the signal. Nearby points have a larger shift and tolerate the same pixel error better.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let the true disparity be \(d\) and the measured disparity \(d+\delta\). Here \(\delta\) is a \sphinxstylestrong{disparity error}, not automatically the error in one particular image coordinate. Since \(d=u_L-u_R\), measurement errors \(\epsilon_L,\epsilon_R\) give \(\delta=\epsilon_L-\epsilon_R\). If the left coordinate is held fixed, a right\sphinxhyphen{}coordinate error has the opposite sign to \(\delta\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Define \sphinxstylestrong{signed depth error} as estimated depth minus true depth. Start with the two depths, give their fractions a common denominator, and simplify:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\begin{aligned}
\Delta Z&=\widehat Z-Z=\frac{fb}{d+\delta}-\frac{fb}{d}\\
&=\frac{fb\,d-fb(d+\delta)}{d(d+\delta)}\\
&=\frac{fb\,d-fb\,d-fb\,\delta}{d(d+\delta)}
=-\frac{fb\,\delta}{d(d+\delta)}.
\end{aligned}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Read the sign:} \(\delta>0\) means too much disparity and an estimate too near (\(\Delta Z<0\)). \(\delta<0\) means too little disparity and an estimate too far (\(\Delta Z>0\)), provided measured disparity stays positive.

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — exact and first\sphinxhyphen{}order depth error}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture04/stereo:eq-lec04-depth-error}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\Delta Z&=\frac{fb}{d+\delta}-\frac{fb}{d}
=-\frac{fb\,\delta}{d(d+\delta)},\\
\Delta Z&\approx-\frac{fb}{d^2}\delta\quad (|\delta|\ll d),\qquad
\frac{|\Delta Z|}{Z}\approx\frac{|\delta|}{d},\\
\left|\frac{dZ}{dd}\right|&=\frac{fb}{d^2}=\frac{Z^2}{fb}.
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Require \(d>0\) and \(d+\delta>0\) for two finite forward\sphinxhyphen{}depth estimates. The approximation is the derivative of \(fb/d\) times \(\delta\). Its magnitude is often quoted without the minus sign; retain the sign when explaining whether the point moves nearer or farther.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Report uncertainty honestly}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Input:} \(f,b,d\) and a signed disparity error \(\delta\).

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the true and estimated depths; subtract for an exact error.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the derivative only when \(|\delta|/d\) is small; label it an approximation.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Check:} overestimating positive disparity makes depth too small. Underestimating it makes depth too large, by a larger magnitude for equal\sphinxhyphen{}size errors.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For bounded error \(|\delta|\le\epsilon<d\), the possible depths lie between \(fb/(d+\epsilon)\) and \(fb/(d-\epsilon)\). If the interval reaches zero disparity, there is no finite upper depth bound under this model.

\end{TextbookBox}


\subsubsection{Understand the approximation, not just the formula}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:understand-the-approximation-not-just-the-formula}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Write \(Z=fb\,d^{-1}\). Differentiating with respect to disparity gives
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{dZ}{dd}=fb(-d^{-2})=-\frac{fb}{d^2}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A derivative is the \sphinxstylestrong{local slope}: approximately how much depth changes for a small change in disparity. Multiply this slope by \(\delta\) to get \(\Delta Z\approx-fb\delta/d^2\). Its units are length per pixel times pixels, giving length.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can also see the approximation without calculus. If \(|\delta|\) is much smaller than \(d\), replace the exact denominator \(d(d+\delta)\) by \(d^2\). Dividing the resulting error magnitude by \(Z=fb/d\) gives
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{|\Delta Z|}{Z}\approx
\frac{fb|\delta|}{d^2}\frac{d}{fb}=\frac{|\delta|}{d}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{A 1\sphinxhyphen{}pixel error at 25 pixels is roughly a 4\% depth error. At 5 pixels it is roughly 20\%.} Close to zero disparity, this approximation becomes unreliable; use the exact depths instead.


\subsubsection{Why distance makes sensitivity grow so quickly}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:why-distance-makes-sensitivity-grow-so-quickly}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Substitute \(d=fb/Z\) into the slope magnitude:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left|\frac{dZ}{dd}\right|
=\frac{fb}{(fb/Z)^2}=\frac{Z^2}{fb}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
At fixed focal length and baseline, \sphinxstylestrong{double the true depth → about four times the absolute error} for the same small disparity error. At fixed true depth, a larger baseline or longer pixel focal length reduces this local sensitivity. A larger baseline also makes occlusions and matching more difficult; geometry alone does not guarantee a usable correspondence.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \(f=50\) pixels and \(b=10\,\mathrm{cm}\), so \(fb=500\):

\subsubsection{A bounded error gives a depth interval}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:a-bounded-error-gives-a-depth-interval}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Suppose \(d=5\) pixels and the disparity error is at most \(0.5\) pixel. With \(fb=500\), the permitted measured disparities are \([4.5,5.5]\). Because larger disparity means smaller depth, reverse the endpoints:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\widehat Z\in
\left[\frac{500}{5.5},\frac{500}{4.5}\right]
=[90.9091,111.1111]\,\mathrm{cm}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Relative to the true depth \(100\,\mathrm{cm}\), the errors lie in \([-9.0909,+11.1111]\,\mathrm{cm}\). The derivative estimate would give approximately \(\pm10\,\mathrm{cm}\). A bound is an interval, not a probability statement. If permitted disparity reaches zero, finite upper depth is no longer bounded.

\subsection{Convert a permitted depth range into search limits}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo:convert-a-permitted-depth-range-into-search-limits}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — disparity search from a depth interval}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture04/stereo:eq-lec04-disparity-range}
\begin{split}0<Z_{\min}\le Z\le Z_{\max}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\frac{fb}{Z_{\max}}\le d\le\frac{fb}{Z_{\min}}.\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The inequalities reverse because depth and positive disparity are inversely related. Use consistent length units and the corrected disparity convention when principal points differ.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Limit the stereo search}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Convert \(b,Z_{\min},Z_{\max}\) to the same length unit.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the continuous disparity endpoints.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For integer hypotheses inside that interval, use the ceiling of the lower endpoint and floor of the upper endpoint. If subpixel or calibration uncertainty matters, include an appropriate margin before discretizing.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check that the larger disparity belongs to the nearer depth.

\end{enumerate}

\end{TextbookBox}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Worked example 4.8 — restrict the Fall 2025 search.} {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:quiz-4-q2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Read the original problem and every worked step}}}}.

\section{Find matches across an image}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:find-matches-across-an-image}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:lec04-matching}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Geometry narrows the search to a row. \sphinxstylestrong{Appearance chooses a position along it.} That is still difficult: repeated textures can look identical, flat regions have little evidence, and some pixels are visible in only one camera.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Source:} lecture PDF pages 42–77, printed slides 46–81 except unnumbered PDF page 54. Stereo contributors named on PDF page 42: Rick Szeliski, Pascal Fua, P. Mordohai, and E. Dunn.


\subsection{Generate, evaluate, select}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:generate-evaluate-select}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The slide sequence on pages 45–53 follows one practical pipeline:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Generate hypotheses:} sample possible disparities or depths. Each projects the reference pixel to a candidate in another view.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Evaluate:} compare image appearance at the candidate, then combine neighboring evidence.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Select:} choose a supported hypothesis, or reject the pixel when evidence is unreliable.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A \sphinxstylestrong{cost volume} stores one score for each image position and hypothesis: dimensions width × height × number of disparities. A depth map selects one hypothesis per reference pixel; it is view\sphinxhyphen{}dependent and need not contain occluded surfaces. The {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture01/motivation::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{earlier reconstruction pipeline}}}} explains how depth can feed other 3D representations.

\index{Cost volume@\spxentry{Cost volume}}\ignorespaces
\index{Photo\sphinxhyphen{}consistency@\spxentry{Photo\sphinxhyphen{}consistency}}\ignorespaces
\index{Occlusion@\spxentry{Occlusion}}\ignorespaces
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — aggregate costs and select disparity}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture04/matching:eq-lec04-cost-volume}
\begin{split}\overline C(p,d)=\frac1{|\Omega_p|}\sum_{q\in\Omega_p}C(q,d),
\qquad \widehat d(p)\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{d\in D_p}\overline C(p,d).\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(p,q\) are pixel positions, \(D_p\) the allowed disparity set, and \(\Omega_p\) a support window. \(C(q,d)\) is a dissimilarity between left location \(q\) and right location \(q-(d,0)\). Require valid samples and nonempty support. An argmin can contain several disparities: a tie is evidence of ambiguity, not a unique measurement.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Build a simple dense stereo estimate}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Input:} rectified images and the permitted disparity range.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Evaluate a cost at every valid candidate. Stack these candidate costs into the volume.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Aggregate support and pick the smallest cost; retain a confidence measure such as separation from competing minima.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Reject inconsistent left–right matches and occlusions. Convert reliable disparities to depth.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is \sphinxstylestrong{winner\sphinxhyphen{}take\sphinxhyphen{}all} selection. The slides also name feature/edge matching followed by interpolation and joint optimization using iterative updates, dynamic programming, energy minimization, or graph methods. Those alternatives add spatial reasoning; they do not make missing image evidence appear.

\end{TextbookBox}

Extracted photographs with original project labels; individual photography credits and reuse terms are not identified on the slide.}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:fig-lec04-pair}}\end{figure}


\subsection{Compare patches, not isolated colors}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:compare-patches-not-isolated-colors}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Photo\sphinxhyphen{}consistency} means that projections of the same scene point have compatible image appearance under the chosen model. For a patch, write its paired samples as \(L_i,R_i(d)\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\).

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — SAD, SSD, and zero\sphinxhyphen{}mean NCC}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture04/matching:eq-lec04-patch-costs}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{SAD}(d)&=\sum_i|L_i-R_i(d)|,\qquad
\operatorname{SSD}(d)=\sum_i(L_i-R_i(d))^2,\\
\operatorname{NCC}(d)&=
\frac{\sum_i(L_i-\overline L)(R_i(d)-\overline R(d))}
{\sqrt{\sum_i(L_i-\overline L)^2\sum_i(R_i(d)-\overline R(d))^2}}.
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\overline L,\overline R\) are patch means. Minimize SAD/SSD; \sphinxstylestrong{maximize} NCC, or minimize a cost such as \(1-\operatorname{NCC}\). NCC lies in \([-1,1]\) for nonconstant patches and is undefined if either centered patch has zero norm. SAD uses intensity units, SSD squared intensity units, NCC is dimensionless.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Choose and check a patch score}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the same valid support and disparity convention for each candidate.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For SAD/SSD, compare aligned intensities directly. SSD penalizes large differences more strongly.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For NCC, subtract each patch’s own mean and divide by its centered norm. Reject near\sphinxhyphen{}zero\sphinxhyphen{}variance supports.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Inspect the full score curve: multiple similar peaks or minima indicate uncertainty.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Positive affine brightness changes preserve ideal NCC, but clipping, reflections, shadows, and nonuniform exposure can break that assumption. The source’s formula image leaves normalization factors dependent on its standard\sphinxhyphen{}deviation convention; the explicit sum\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}squares denominator above avoids that ambiguity.

\end{TextbookBox}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Raw difference scores favor B. For NCC, A’s centered values equal the reference’s \((-10,0,10)\), giving correlation one. B’s centered values are \((-10/3,20/3,-10/3)\), perpendicular to the reference vector, giving zero. NCC favors A under the uniform brightness\sphinxhyphen{}offset model.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A flat patch such as \((20,20,20)\) instead has zero centered norm. It cannot supply a defined NCC score or a distinctive texture match.

\end{TextbookBox}


\subsection{Window size trades detail for support}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:window-size-trades-detail-for-support}}
\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.850\linewidth]{{window-size}.png}
\caption{The source’s \(w=3\) versus \(w=20\) results, left to right (PDF page 66, printed slide 70). Larger support suppresses isolated mistakes but can erase detail. Extracted source illustration; its individual creator and reuse terms are not identified on that slide.}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:fig-lec04-window-size}}\end{figure}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A constant\sphinxhyphen{}disparity window assumes \sphinxstylestrong{fronto\sphinxhyphen{}parallel support}: one axial depth. Slanted surfaces violate this assumption; windows crossing foreground and background mix different depths.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.850\linewidth]{{support-boundary}.pdf}
\caption{A larger window can vote for two different depths. Adapting its position or weights changes which surface contributes evidence.}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:fig-lec04-support}}\end{figure}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The slides offer several ways to adapt support:
\begin{itemize}
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Shiftable windows:} choose among windows that contain the reference pixel; favor support that stays on one surface.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Rod\sphinxhyphen{}shaped supports:} test elongated directions that may follow an approximately constant\sphinxhyphen{}disparity contour.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Adaptive weights:} downweight neighbors far away in position or color.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Oriented\sphinxhyphen{}plane hypotheses:} allow disparity to vary across a slanted plane instead of assuming one constant value.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
All add assumptions. Similar colors can still occur at different depths, and an image edge need not be a depth edge.


\subsection{Rank and Census use relative intensity order}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:rank-and-census-use-relative-intensity-order}}
\index{Census transform@\spxentry{Census transform}}\ignorespaces
\index{Rank transform@\spxentry{Rank transform}}\ignorespaces
\index{Adaptive support@\spxentry{Adaptive support}}\ignorespaces
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — rank, Census, and Hamming distance}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture04/matching:eq-lec04-census}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
r(p)&=\sum_{q\in\mathcal N_p}\mathbf1[I(q)<I(p)],\\
\mathcal C(p)&=\bigl(\mathbf1[I(q_1)<I(p)],\ldots,
\mathbf1[I(q_m)<I(p)]\bigr),\\
H(\mathcal C_L,\mathcal C_R)&=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbf1[\mathcal C_{L,i}\ne\mathcal C_{R,i}].
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\mathcal N_p\) contains \(m\) ordered neighbors excluding the center; \(\mathbf1[\cdot]\) is one when its condition is true and zero otherwise. Rank ranges from \(0\) to \(m\); Census keeps the complete ordered bit string. Use the same neighbor order and tie convention in both images. Both preserve strictly increasing intensity remappings within the compared support.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Match relative\sphinxhyphen{}intensity patterns}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compare each neighbor with the center using the fixed strict inequality.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Sum the comparisons for rank, or retain their order for Census.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compare rank\sphinxhyphen{}transformed images with a difference cost; compare Census strings by Hamming distance.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check for repeated patterns and ties. Relative order is robust to some brightness changes, not to all lighting or geometry changes.

\end{enumerate}

\end{TextbookBox}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:ex-lec04-census}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Worked example 4.10 — equal ranks can hide different patterns}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Original companion to:} PDF page 74, printed slide 78.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let the center intensity be 20. Ordered neighbors \((10,30,15,25)\) give Census \sphinxstylestrong{1010} and rank 2. A second patch with center 20 and neighbors \((5,10,30,40)\) gives \sphinxstylestrong{1100}, also rank 2. Their Census Hamming distance is \sphinxstylestrong{2}: bits 2 and 3 disagree.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The rank compresses spatial evidence into one count. Census retains which neighbors were darker. Adding the same brightness offset to every pixel of either patch preserves its comparisons, provided clipping does not change them.

\end{TextbookBox}


\subsection{Give nearby, similar neighbors more influence}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:give-nearby-similar-neighbors-more-influence}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Formula — locally adaptive support}\par\smallskip
\begin{equation}\label{equation:lectures/lecture04/matching:eq-lec04-adaptive}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\Delta_c(p,q)&=\|\operatorname{Lab}(p)-\operatorname{Lab}(q)\|_2,
\quad \Delta_s(p,q)=\|p-q\|_2,\\
w(p,q)&=\exp\left[-\frac{\Delta_c(p,q)}{\gamma_c}
-\frac{\Delta_s(p,q)}{\gamma_s}\right],\\
\overline C_w(p,d)&=\frac{\sum_{q\in\Omega_p}w(p,q)C(q,d)}
{\sum_{q\in\Omega_p}w(p,q)}.
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\operatorname{Lab}(p)=(L_p,a_p,b_p)^T\) is a three\sphinxhyphen{}channel color vector. \(\gamma_c>0\) uses color\sphinxhyphen{}distance units; \(\gamma_s>0\) uses pixels, making both exponents dimensionless. These are reference\sphinxhyphen{}image weights with a nonzero sum. Other methods also include shifted right\sphinxhyphen{}image weights; specify the convention. A common weight multiplier cancels.

\end{TextbookBox}

\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Aggregate without crossing every edge equally}\par\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute color distance in CIE Lab and spatial distance within the support.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Calculate positive weights with the chosen scales.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Form a weighted average cost for each disparity and compare candidates.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Inspect whether the support follows actual surfaces. Color similarity helps; it does not prove shared depth.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
PDF pages 52/76 credit Yoon and Kweon (PAMI 2006); page 53 credits Lu et al. (CVPR 2013) for an oriented\sphinxhyphen{}plane extension. These descriptions explain their roles; they do not reproduce the full methods.

\end{TextbookBox}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching:ex-lec04-adaptive}}
\begin{TextbookBox}
\textbf{Worked example 4.11 — a two\sphinxhyphen{}sample depth boundary}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Original companion to:} PDF pages 75–76.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Two support samples are each one pixel away. One has the same color as the reference; the other differs by 40 Lab units. With \(\gamma_c=10\), \(\gamma_s=2\), their weights are \(e^{-0.5}\approx0.60653\) and \(e^{-4.5}\approx0.01111\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
At the true disparity, their costs are \((0,10)\); at a wrong disparity, \((10,0)\). Uniform averaging ties both at 5. Adaptive averaging gives about \sphinxstylestrong{0.180} for the true disparity and \sphinxstylestrong{9.820} for the wrong one. The same\sphinxhyphen{}color sample now contributes most of the evidence.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If that color boundary did not correspond to a depth boundary, this weighting preference could be misleading. The source’s result images compare such support choices, not a universal guarantee of correctness.

\end{TextbookBox}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The slide list also names \sphinxstylestrong{mutual information} (statistical dependence between intensities) and \sphinxstylestrong{learning\sphinxhyphen{}based methods} (learned appearance features or costs). They change how hypotheses are scored. The same geometry, visibility limits, and need to recognize uncertain matches remain.

\subsubsection{Problem 1}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:problem-1}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:quiz-1-q1}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:ex-lec04-symbolic}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original problem · quiz booklet}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(x_A=(x,y,w)^T\) be a point in image A and \(F_{AB}=[f_{ij}]\) be the fundamental matrix from image A to B. Write the epipolar\sphinxhyphen{}line equation in B, using both matrix entries and the row vectors \(\mathbf f_1^T,\mathbf f_2^T,\mathbf f_3^T\). Make an illustrative sketch.

\par\medskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Given / relevant facts:}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
F_{AB}=\begin{bmatrix}f_{11}&f_{12}&f_{13}\\f_{21}&f_{22}&f_{23}\\f_{31}&f_{32}&f_{33}\end{bmatrix}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A homogeneous line is \(\ell_B=(a,b,c)^T\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Fully worked solution} — red labels explain the step; blue mathematics shows the calculation.

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Choose the point\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}line rule}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} F maps the known point to possible matches in the other image.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Start from the fundamental\sphinxhyphen{}matrix point\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}line relation: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\ell_B=F_{AB}x_A\)}. This is a line, not the matched pixel itself.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Multiply all three rows}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The resulting column contains line coefficients.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Multiply each row of the full matrix by the input column:
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\begin{aligned}
\ell_B&=\begin{pmatrix}f_{11}&f_{12}&f_{13}\\f_{21}&f_{22}&f_{23}\\f_{31}&f_{32}&f_{33}\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\w\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\begin{pmatrix}f_{11}x+f_{12}y+f_{13}w\\f_{21}x+f_{22}y+f_{23}w\\f_{31}x+f_{32}y+f_{33}w\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf f_1^Tx_A\\\mathbf f_2^Tx_A\\\mathbf f_3^Tx_A\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The output entries are line coefficients {\color{QuizMathBlue} \((a,b,c)^T\)}, not point coordinates.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 3 — Enforce point\sphinxhyphen{}line incidence}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} A true candidate must give a zero scalar dot product.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A candidate {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(x_B=(u_B,v_B,w_B)^T\)} lies on that line when its dot product is zero:
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\begin{aligned}
0=x_B^T\ell_B
&=(f_{11}x+f_{12}y+f_{13}w)u_B\\
&\quad +(f_{21}x+f_{22}y+f_{23}w)v_B\\
&\quad +(f_{31}x+f_{32}y+f_{33}w)w_B.
\end{aligned}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For a finite point set {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(w_B=1\)}, giving {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(au_B+bv_B+c=0\)}. If {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(b\ne0\)}, rewrite it as {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(v_B=-(a/b)u_B-c/b\)} for plotting; {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(b=0\)} instead gives a vertical line when {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(a\ne0\)}.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 4 — Draw the predicted line}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} One point generally predicts a line rather than a unique match.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the point is finite, set {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(w_B=1\)}; plot {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(au_B+bv_B+c=0\)}. For {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(b\neq0\)}, {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(v_B=-(a/b)u_B-c/b\)}. Draw a line in image B through the unknown match; its exact location depends on the supplied {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(F_{AB}\)} and {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(x_A\)}.

\par

\subsubsection{Problem 2}

\par\medskip\textbf{Original problem · quiz booklet}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
Write the explicit epipolar constraint \(x_B^TF_{AB}x_A=0\) for \(x_A=(1,0,1)^T\) and \(x_B=(0,1,1)^T\). Rewrite it using row\sphinxhyphen{}vector dot products.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The zero middle coordinate removes the second column’s contribution.

&=\begin{pmatrix}f_{11}(1)+f_{12}(0)+f_{13}(1)\\f_{21}(1)+f_{22}(0)+f_{23}(1)\\f_{31}(1)+f_{32}(0)+f_{33}(1)\end{pmatrix}

\end{aligned}

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}

\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The compact row notation must express the same scalar equation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Rewrite using the supplied row vectors: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(x_B^TFx_A=(\mathbf f_2^T+\mathbf f_3^T)x_A=\mathbf f_2\cdot x_A+\mathbf f_3\cdot x_A=0\)}.

{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 4 — Make the requested sketch}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The camera rays and image line explain the algebra geometrically.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Sketch two camera centers joined by a baseline, their image planes, a common 3D point and both rays; label the line in image B that contains the possible match. The same diagram as on the preceding page applies.

\par

\subsubsection{Problem 2}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:quiz-2-q2}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:id2}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original problem · quiz booklet}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \(x_A=(1,0,1)^T\) and \(x_B=(0,1,1)^T\), expand \(x_B^TF_{AB}x_A=0\) and express it in terms of row vectors.

\par\medskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Fully worked solution} — red labels explain the step; blue mathematics shows the calculation.

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Multiply the known point into F}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} This selects and adds columns one and three.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Multiply the actual point into the full symbolic matrix:
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\begin{aligned}
F_{AB}x_A&=\begin{pmatrix}f_{11}&f_{12}&f_{13}\\f_{21}&f_{22}&f_{23}\\f_{31}&f_{32}&f_{33}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\begin{pmatrix}f_{11}(1)+f_{12}(0)+f_{13}(1)\\f_{21}(1)+f_{22}(0)+f_{23}(1)\\f_{31}(1)+f_{32}(0)+f_{33}(1)\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}f_{11}+f_{13}\\f_{21}+f_{23}\\f_{31}+f_{33}\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Perform the final row\sphinxhyphen{}column product}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Only two output coefficients contribute.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Transpose the other point and multiply the row by that column:
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\begin{aligned}
x_B^TF_{AB}x_A
&=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}f_{11}+f_{13}\\f_{21}+f_{23}\\f_{31}+f_{33}\end{pmatrix}\\
&=0(f_{11}+f_{13})+1(f_{21}+f_{23})+1(f_{31}+f_{33}).
\end{aligned}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The result is a scalar: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \((1\times3)(3\times1)=1\times1\)}.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 3 — Enforce the zero constraint}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Correspondence requires incidence, not equality between a point and a line.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Set the scalar to zero: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\boxed{f_{21}+f_{23}+f_{31}+f_{33}=0}\)}.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 4 — Express the row\sphinxhyphen{}vector form}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} This checks the equivalent notation requested by the quiz.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In row notation, {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\boxed{(\mathbf f_2^T+\mathbf f_3^T)x_A=0}\)}; this is one scalar epipolar incidence constraint.

\par


\subsection{Fall 2025 Quiz 2 — Three\sphinxhyphen{}view epipolar geometry}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:fall-2025-quiz-2-three-view-epipolar-geometry}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:quiz-source-3}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Historical source:} \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{3dcvMid/quizzesf25sol/cs532f25\_quiz\_2\_solution.pdf}}.


\subsubsection{Question 1}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:question-1}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:quiz-3-q1}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:ex-lec04-third-view}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original problem · quiz booklet}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
Three images A, B, C observe a point. The pair \(x_A\leftrightarrow x_B\) is known, but its image location \(x_C\) is unknown. Given fundamental matrices \(F_{AC}\) and \(F_{BC}\) (which map A/B points to lines in C), determine \(x_C\).

\par\medskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Fully worked solution} — red labels explain the step; blue mathematics shows the calculation.

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Predict the line from image A}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The unknown point in C must satisfy the A\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}C geometry.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Map {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(x_A\)} to a line in C: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\boxed{\ell_C^{(A)}=F_{AC}x_A}\)}. Any correct {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(x_C\)} must satisfy {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(x_C^T\ell_C^{(A)}=0\)}.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Predict the line from image B}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} A second independent view supplies another constraint in the same image C.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Map {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(x_B\)} independently to a second line in C: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\boxed{\ell_C^{(B)}=F_{BC}x_B}\)}. The same {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(x_C\)} must satisfy {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(x_C^T\ell_C^{(B)}=0\)}.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 3 — Intersect the two lines}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Their cross product gives the homogeneous intersection.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the projective plane, the intersection of two lines is their cross product:
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\boxed{x_C\sim \ell_C^{(A)}\times\ell_C^{(B)}}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 4 — Normalize and check the intersection}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Homogeneous coordinates must be converted before reading a finite pixel.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Normalize {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(x_C=(q_1,q_2,q_3)^T\)} to {\color{QuizMathBlue} \((q_1/q_3,q_2/q_3)\)} if {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(q_3\ne0\)}. Check both incidence products equal zero. If the two lines coincide, they do not determine a unique point; with noisy lines use an appropriate least\sphinxhyphen{}squares estimate.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 5 — Define a numerical companion}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The original symbolic question has no numerical matrices to multiply.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Original numerical companion: let {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(x_A=(1/2,3/4,1)^T\)}, {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(x_B=(1/4,3/4,1)^T\)}, and
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
F_{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&-1\\0&0&0\\1&0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
F_{BC}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&-1\\0&0&-1\\1&1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These are compatible with identity\sphinxhyphen{}oriented normalized cameras centered at {\color{QuizMathBlue} \((0,0,0)\)}, {\color{QuizMathBlue} \((1,0,0)\)}, {\color{QuizMathBlue} \((0,1,0)\)} observing world point {\color{QuizMathBlue} \((2,3,4)\)}.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 6 — Multiply both numerical matrices}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Full row products show exactly where both predicted lines come from.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Multiply both matrices, retaining every row operation:
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\begin{aligned}
\ell_C^{(A)}&=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&-1\\0&0&0\\1&0&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1/2\\3/4\\1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}0(1/2)+0(3/4)-1\\0\\1(1/2)+0+0\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\\1/2\end{pmatrix},\\
\ell_C^{(B)}&=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&-1\\0&0&-1\\1&1&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1/4\\3/4\\1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-1\\1/4+3/4\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 7 — Expand the cross product}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Its three components determine the common image point.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Intersect the two lines by expanding the cross product:
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
x_C\sim\begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\\1/2\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}0(1)-(1/2)(-1)\\(1/2)(-1)-(-1)(1)\\(-1)(-1)-0(-1)\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}1/2\\1/2\\1\end{pmatrix}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Divide by the last coordinate to get {\color{QuizMathBlue} \((u_C,v_C)=(1/2,1/2)\)}. A scaled result {\color{QuizMathBlue} \((4,4,8)^T\)} gives the same ratios.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 8 — Substitute into both lines}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Both independent constraints must pass at the answer.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Check both original line equations at the answer:
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\begin{aligned}
(\ell_C^{(A)})^Tx_C&=(-1)(1/2)+0(1/2)+(1/2)(1)=0,\\
(\ell_C^{(B)})^Tx_C&=(-1)(1/2)+(-1)(1/2)+(1)(1)=0.
\end{aligned}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Coincident lines give a zero cross product and no unique point. Distinct parallel lines meet at infinity; nearly parallel lines make a finite intersection sensitive to noise. Image appearance must still confirm visibility and identity.

\par

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.700\linewidth]{{third-view}.pdf}
\caption{The two numerical companion lines intersect at the predicted third\sphinxhyphen{}image point.}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:id8}}\end{figure}


\subsubsection{Question 2}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:question-2}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:quiz-3-q2}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:ex-lec04-invalid-f}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original problem · quiz booklet}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
Given \(x'=(1,2,1)^T\) and
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
F=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&1\\0&1&2\\1&0&1\end{bmatrix}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
, propose an epipolar\sphinxhyphen{}consistent point \(x\).

\par\medskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Fully worked solution} — red labels explain the step; blue mathematics shows the calculation.

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Choose the unprimed\sphinxhyphen{}image line}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The transpose maps the primed point back to a line in the unprimed image.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Start from {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\boxed{x'^TFx=0}\)}. To obtain the possible locations of {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(x\)}, form the line {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\ell=F^Tx'\)} in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{unprimed} image.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Transpose and multiply explicitly}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The line coefficients come from row\sphinxhyphen{}column products.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Transpose explicitly, then multiply row by row:
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
F^T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\2&1&0\\1&2&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
F^Tx'=\begin{pmatrix}1(1)+0(2)+1(1)\\2(1)+1(2)+0(1)\\1(1)+2(2)+1(1)\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}2\\4\\6\end{pmatrix}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 3 — Write the incidence equation}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} A candidate must make the dot product zero.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Write line incidence for {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(x=(u,v,1)^T\)}: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(2u+4v+6=0\)}, or {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\boxed{u+2v+3=0}\)}.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 4 — Choose a convenient finite point}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} One free coordinate remains because the answer is a whole line.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Choose a convenient solution, e.g. {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(v=0\Rightarrow u=-3\)}. Thus {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\boxed{x=(-3,0,1)^T}\)}. Alternatively {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(u=-1\Rightarrow v=-1\)}.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 5 — Check the answer and the matrix rank}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Solving the given equation does not make an invalid matrix physically valid.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Verify the point by multiplying it into the original supplied matrix:
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
Fx=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\0&1&2\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}-3\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}-3+0+1\\0+0+2\\-3+0+1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\2\\-2\end{pmatrix},
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
x'^TFx=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}-2\\2\\-2\end{pmatrix}=-2+4-2=0.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
But {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\det F=1(1)-2(-2)+1(-1)=4\)}, so its rank is three. The point solves the supplied equation; this matrix is not a valid fundamental matrix for pinhole cameras.

\par

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Source check / assumptions:} The uploaded solution writes \(x'^TF=x\); that is dimensionally/conceptually inaccurate. \(x'^TF\) is a \sphinxstyleemphasis{line row\sphinxhyphen{}vector}, not a specific corresponding image point. There are infinitely many epipolar\sphinxhyphen{}consistent points on this line. Note that a true fundamental matrix must have rank 2; the numerical matrix given in the quiz is nonsingular, but its scalar incidence equation remains solvable as requested.


\subsection{Fall 2025 Quiz 3 — Stereo depth sensitivity}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:fall-2025-quiz-3-stereo-depth-sensitivity}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:quiz-source-4}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Historical source:} \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{3dcvMid/quizzesf25sol/cs532f25\_quiz\_3\_solution.pdf}}.


\subsubsection{Question 1}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:quiz-4-q1}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:ex-lec04-stereo-fall}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:id3}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original problem · quiz booklet}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
Rectified stereo cameras have baseline \(b=10\) cm, common focal length \(f=50\) pixels, and true disparity \(d^*=25\) pixels. Determine the depth error caused by a 1\sphinxhyphen{}pixel disparity mistake.

\par\medskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Given / relevant facts:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use \(Z=bf/d\). The problem does not say whether disparity is over\sphinxhyphen{} or underestimated, so compute both; the supplied key uses a first\sphinxhyphen{}order approximate magnitude.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Fully worked solution} — red labels explain the step; blue mathematics shows the calculation.

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Compute the true depth}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} We need a reference before defining an error.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Keep physical units consistent: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(bf=(10\,\mathrm{cm})(50\,\mathrm{px})=500\,\mathrm{cm\,px}\)}. True depth:
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
Z^*=500/25=\boxed{20\,\mathrm{cm}}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Calculate the underestimated\sphinxhyphen{}disparity case}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} A smaller positive disparity should reconstruct a farther point.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\delta=-1\)}, measured disparity is {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(24\)} pixels:
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\widehat Z_- =\frac{500}{24}=\frac{125}{6}\,\mathrm{cm},\qquad
\Delta Z_- =\frac{125}{6}-20=\frac{125-120}{6}=\frac56\,\mathrm{cm}\approx+0.83333\,\mathrm{cm}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 3 — Calculate the overestimated\sphinxhyphen{}disparity case}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} A larger disparity should reconstruct a nearer point.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\delta=+1\)}, measured disparity is {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(26\)} pixels:
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\widehat Z_+ =\frac{500}{26}=\frac{250}{13}\,\mathrm{cm},\qquad
\Delta Z_+ =\frac{250}{13}-20=\frac{250-260}{13}=-\frac{10}{13}\,\mathrm{cm}\approx-0.76923\,\mathrm{cm}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 4 — Compare the first\sphinxhyphen{}order approximation}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The derivative estimates a small change rather than both exact nonlinear errors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To obtain the first\sphinxhyphen{}order approximation, differentiate {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(Z(d)=bf/d\)}:
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\frac{dZ}{dd}=-\frac{bf}{d^2},\quad \Delta Z\approx-\frac{500}{25^2}\Delta d=-0.8\Delta d\ \mathrm{cm}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus the \sphinxstyleemphasis{approximate magnitude} is {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\boxed{0.8\,\mathrm{cm}}\)} for {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(|\Delta d|=1\)}.

\par

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Source check / assumptions:} The exact errors are asymmetric (\(+0.8333\) and \(-0.7692\) cm), whereas the linearized approximation gives \(\pm0.8\) cm. The source key reports the approximation, not both exact cases.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.700\linewidth]{{depth-sensitivity}.pdf}
\caption{The same pixel error produces much larger depth errors at smaller disparity.}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:id9}}\end{figure}


\subsubsection{Question 2}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:quiz-4-q2}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:ex-lec04-search}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:id4}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original problem · quiz booklet}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the same setup, restrict the searched 3D depth range to between 1 m and 5 m. What disparity interval corresponds to this?

\par\medskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Fully worked solution} — red labels explain the step; blue mathematics shows the calculation.

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Convert the baseline to meters}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Depth and baseline must use the same physical unit.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Convert baseline: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(b=10\,\mathrm{cm}=0.1\,\mathrm m\)}. Then {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(bf=0.1(50)=5\,\mathrm{m\,px}\)}.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Invert the depth formula}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Search limits are requested in disparity rather than depth.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Invert the depth equation: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(d=bf/Z\)}. Larger depth implies smaller disparity.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 3 — Evaluate the far endpoint}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The farthest permitted point gives the smallest positive disparity.

\sphinxAtStartPar
At farthest depth {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(Z_{\max}=5\)} m: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(d_{\min}=5/5=\boxed{1\,\mathrm{px}}\)}.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 4 — Evaluate the near endpoint}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The nearest permitted point gives the largest disparity.

\sphinxAtStartPar
At nearest depth {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(Z_{\min}=1\)} m: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(d_{\max}=5/1=\boxed{5\,\mathrm{px}}\)}. Search {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\boxed{d\in[1,5]\,\mathrm{px}}\)}.

\par


\subsection{Spring 2019 Quiz 5 — Exact stereo errors}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:spring-2019-quiz-5-exact-stereo-errors}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:quiz-source-5}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Historical source:} \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{3dcvMid/olderquizzes/cs532s19\_quiz5\sphinxhyphen{}2.pdf}}.


\subsubsection{Problem 1(a–c)}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:problem-1-ac}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:quiz-5-q1}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:ex-lec04-stereo-spring}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original problem · quiz booklet}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
Rectified cameras have baseline \(b=10\) cm and focal length \(f=5\) pixels. True disparity is \(d^*=3\) pixels. (a) Find the depth error when disparity is underestimated by one pixel; (b) when overestimated by one pixel; (c) explain whether these errors remain constant at larger disparity.

\par\medskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Fully worked solution} — red labels explain the step; blue mathematics shows the calculation.

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Insert focal length and baseline}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Their product determines the depth scale.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Write the depth\sphinxhyphen{}disparity law and insert the givens: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(Z(d)=bf/d=(10)(5)/d=50/d\ \mathrm{cm}\)}.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Compute the true depth}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Signed errors are measured relative to this value.

\sphinxAtStartPar
True depth is {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(Z^*=50/3=\boxed{16\tfrac23\,\mathrm{cm}}\approx16.6667\)} cm.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 3 — Underestimate disparity by one}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Subtract exact fractions before rounding the error.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Underestimate disparity by one: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\widehat d=3-1=2\)}. Then
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\widehat Z=\frac{50}{2}=25\,\mathrm{cm},\qquad
\Delta Z=25-\frac{50}{3}=\frac{75-50}{3}=\frac{25}{3}\,\mathrm{cm}\approx+8.3333\,\mathrm{cm}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A positive signed error means the estimated point is too far away.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 4 — Overestimate disparity by one}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The nonlinear inverse relation produces a different error magnitude.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Overestimate disparity by one: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\widehat d=3+1=4\)}. Then
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\widehat Z=\frac{50}{4}=\frac{25}{2}\,\mathrm{cm},\qquad
\Delta Z=\frac{25}{2}-\frac{50}{3}=\frac{75-100}{6}=-\frac{25}{6}\,\mathrm{cm}\approx-4.1667\,\mathrm{cm}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A negative signed error means the estimate is too near. The two magnitudes are unequal.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 5 — Generalize the two exact errors}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Their denominators show how the magnitudes change with disparity.

\sphinxAtStartPar
No: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(Z(d)=bf/d\)} is nonlinear. The exact error for +1 px is {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(Z(d+1)-Z(d)=-bf/[d(d+1)]\)}; for \sphinxhyphen{}1 px it is {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(Z(d-1)-Z(d)=+bf/[d(d-1)]\)} for {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(d>1\)}. Both magnitudes diminish at larger {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(d\)}.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 6 — Interpret the local derivative}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} It explains the trend for small perturbations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The derivative {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(dZ/dd=-bf/d^2\)} gives the local approximation {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(|\Delta Z|\approx bf|\Delta d|/d^2\)}. Because {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(1/d^2\)} decreases as {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(d\)} grows, disparity errors cause smaller depth errors for nearer points.

\par

\subsubsection{Problem 1(a–c)}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:quiz-6-q1}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:id5}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original problem · quiz booklet}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
Rectified stereo cameras: \(b=10\) cm, \(f=5\) pixels, true \(d^*=3\) pixels. Determine (a) error for \(\hat d=2\), (b) error for \(\hat d=4\), and (c) how errors behave as disparity increases.

\par\medskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Fully worked solution} — red labels explain the step; blue mathematics shows the calculation.

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Set up the stereo depth law}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The same physical and pixel units must be used consistently.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Write {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(Z(d)=bf/d\)}, using {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(bf=(10\,\mathrm{cm})(5\,\mathrm{px})=50\,\mathrm{cm\,px}\)}.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Find the true depth}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} This is the reference for both signed errors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
True depth: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(Z^*=50/3=16.6667\)} cm.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 3 — Solve the smaller\sphinxhyphen{}disparity case}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} A common denominator makes the positive error explicit.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Underestimate disparity by one: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\widehat d=3-1=2\)}. Then
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\widehat Z=\frac{50}{2}=25\,\mathrm{cm},\qquad
\Delta Z=25-\frac{50}{3}=\frac{75-50}{3}=\frac{25}{3}\,\mathrm{cm}\approx+8.3333\,\mathrm{cm}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A positive signed error means the estimated point is too far away.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 4 — Solve the larger\sphinxhyphen{}disparity case}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The exact subtraction exposes the unequal negative error.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Overestimate disparity by one: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\widehat d=3+1=4\)}. Then
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\widehat Z=\frac{50}{4}=\frac{25}{2}\,\mathrm{cm},\qquad
\Delta Z=\frac{25}{2}-\frac{50}{3}=\frac{75-100}{6}=-\frac{25}{6}\,\mathrm{cm}\approx-4.1667\,\mathrm{cm}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A negative signed error means the estimate is too near. The two magnitudes are unequal.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 5 — Explain the asymmetry}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Equal disparity changes do not give equal changes in inverse disparity.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Explain why the two numbers differ: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(Z\)} is proportional to {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(1/d\)}, not linear in {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(d\)}; changes of +1 and \sphinxhyphen{}1 around the same {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(d\)} need not have equal effects.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 6 — State the large\sphinxhyphen{}disparity trend}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The derivative and exact formula both predict decreasing sensitivity.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Generalize: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\frac{dZ}{dd}=-bf/d^2\)}, so a fixed disparity error typically matters less at larger disparities. For exact +1 px, {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\Delta Z=-bf/[d(d+1)]\)}.

\par


\subsection{A4. Essential matrix and cheirality (L4, slides 22–41)}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:a4-essential-matrix-and-cheirality-l4-slides-2241}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:quiz-source-a4}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Original practice from the supplied booklet; not a historical quiz question.}


\subsubsection{Illustrative problem}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:illustrative-problem}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/quiz-workbook:quiz-a4-q1}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original problem · quiz booklet}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
Two calibrated cameras have relative rotation \(R=I\) and translation \(t=(1,0,0)^T\) in compatible normalized units. Form \(E\), identify its rank and singular values, and explain why pose decomposition is not unique without a positive\sphinxhyphen{}depth test.

\par\medskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Fully worked solution} — red labels explain the step; blue mathematics shows the calculation.

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Write the essential\sphinxhyphen{}matrix construction}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Translation and rotation determine the calibrated two\sphinxhyphen{}view relation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The essential matrix is {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\boxed{E=[t]_\times R}\)}, with cross\sphinxhyphen{}product matrix
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
[t]_\times=\begin{bmatrix}0&-t_z&t_y\\t_z&0&-t_x\\-t_y&t_x&0\end{bmatrix}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Insert the translation and rotation}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The cross\sphinxhyphen{}product matrix fixes every entry.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Insert {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(t=(1,0,0)^T\)} and {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(R=I\)}:
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\boxed{E=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&0\\0&0&-1\\0&1&0\end{bmatrix}}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 3 — Multiply E transpose by E}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Its eigenvalues determine E’s singular values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the singular\sphinxhyphen{}value check from the complete product:
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\begin{aligned}
E^TE&=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\0&0&1\\0&-1&0\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\0&0&-1\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Its eigenvalues are {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(1,1,0\)}, so the singular values of {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(E\)} are their nonnegative square roots: {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(1,1,0\)}. Two are nonzero, hence rank two.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 4 — Connect calibrated and pixel coordinates}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Intrinsic matrices convert between the essential and fundamental relations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For calibrated normalized image coordinates {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\hat x,\hat x'\)}, corresponding points satisfy {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\hat x'^TE\hat x=0\)}. If pixel intrinsics are known, {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(E=K_R^TFK_L\)}.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 5 — List the pose ambiguity}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The SVD gives two rotations and two translation signs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Decomposing a general essential matrix via SVD gives two rotation candidates {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(R_1,R_2\)} and a translation \sphinxstyleemphasis{direction} with two signs, i.e. four candidates {\color{QuizMathBlue} \((R_1,+t)\)}, {\color{QuizMathBlue} \((R_1,-t)\)}, {\color{QuizMathBlue} \((R_2,+t)\)}, {\color{QuizMathBlue} \((R_2,-t)\)}.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 6 — Apply the positive\sphinxhyphen{}depth test}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The visible scene must lie in front of both observing cameras.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Triangulate one or more matched 3D points under each candidate. Keep the one for which the points have positive camera\sphinxhyphen{}frame {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(Z\)} in \sphinxstyleemphasis{both} views (cheirality). The magnitude of {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(t\)} remains unobservable without external scale.

\par

\section{TLDR}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:tldr}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:lec04-tldr}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Lecture 4 in one sentence:} estimate valid two\sphinxhyphen{}view geometry, choose a camera pose that sees the scene, and turn reliable stereo matches into depths with honest error estimates.


\subsection{The important things}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:the-important-things}}\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Keep points, lines, and scalars distinct.} A pixel defines a ray; that ray and the baseline define a plane whose intersection with the other image is a line. Compute that line with \(Fx\), then test a candidate using \(x'^TFx=0\). The assigned quizzes practice symbolic expansion and third\sphinxhyphen{}view prediction. Two lines in a third image can locate a point, unless their intersection is degenerate. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/epipolar-practice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{quiz practice}}}}.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Check rank before trusting “F.”} Fall 2025 Quiz 2 supplies a rank\sphinxhyphen{}three matrix. Its bilinear equation can be solved, but it is not valid pinhole\sphinxhyphen{}camera geometry. A noisy estimate requires a rank\sphinxhyphen{}two correction and pixel\sphinxhyphen{}space residual checks. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/estimation::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{estimation}}}}.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Calibration supplies an essential matrix.} \(E=K'^TFK=[t]_\times R\) has equal nonzero singular values and one zero. It recovers translation direction, not metric scale. Numerical conditioning transforms and camera calibration are different operations. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/essential::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{essential geometry}}}}.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Test all four poses.} Two rotations and two translation signs produce four candidates. Positive reconstructed depths in both cameras select the visible configuration for suitable nondegenerate data. Translation \(t\) is not the second camera center.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Disparity is inverse depth.} In the specified rectified convention, \(Z=fb/d\). Use focal length and disparity in pixels, baseline and depth in one length unit. Account for unequal principal\sphinxhyphen{}point columns. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/stereo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{stereo}}}}.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{A one\sphinxhyphen{}pixel depth error is not symmetric.} Underestimating disparity pushes the point farther by more than an equal overestimate pulls it nearer. Use the exact error when the disparity error is a substantial fraction of disparity. Small disparities are especially fragile: local error magnitude is approximately \(Z^2|\delta|/(fb)\). At fixed cameras and small disparity error, doubling depth roughly quadruples absolute error.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Appearance chooses among geometric candidates.} Dense stereo generates hypotheses, evaluates costs, aggregates support, and selects or rejects. Minimize SAD/SSD; maximize NCC. Flat patches, repetitions, and occlusions can defeat a low\sphinxhyphen{}cost match. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/matching::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-doc}{matching}}}}.

\item {}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Support has assumptions.} A constant\sphinxhyphen{}disparity window favors fronto\sphinxhyphen{}parallel surfaces; large windows can mix depths. Shifted, elongated, weighted, or oriented\sphinxhyphen{}plane support can help. Rank retains a count; Census retains the ordered relative\sphinxhyphen{}intensity pattern. None removes ambiguity automatically.

\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Question 1}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:question-1}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:lec04-tldr-q1}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original practice question}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \(x_A=(0,1,1)^T\), \(x_B=(1,0,1)^T\), expand \(x_B^TFx_A\) in matrix entries.

\par\medskip

\par\medskip
\textbf{Worked solution}\par\smallskip

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Multiply the point into F}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The zero first coordinate selects columns two and three.
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\begin{aligned}Fx_A&=\begin{pmatrix}f_{11}&f_{12}&f_{13}\\f_{21}&f_{22}&f_{23}\\f_{31}&f_{32}&f_{33}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\\&=\begin{pmatrix}f_{12}+f_{13}\\f_{22}+f_{23}\\f_{32}+f_{33}\end{pmatrix}.\end{aligned}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Dot with the second point}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Its transpose selects the first and third output entries.
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}f_{12}+f_{13}\\f_{22}+f_{23}\\f_{32}+f_{33}\end{pmatrix}=f_{12}+f_{13}+f_{32}+f_{33}=0.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip


\subsubsection{Question 2}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:question-2}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:lec04-tldr-q2}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original practice question}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
Two predicted lines in image C are proportional. Does their cross product give a unique finite correspondence?

\par\medskip

\par\medskip
\textbf{Worked solution}\par\smallskip

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Write proportional line vectors}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Nonzero scaling represents the same homogeneous line.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\ell_2=k\ell_1\)} with {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(k\ne0\)}. Then {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\ell_1\times\ell_2=k(\ell_1\times\ell_1)=0\)}.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Interpret the zero result}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The zero homogeneous vector cannot represent a unique image point.

\sphinxAtStartPar
No unique finite correspondence is determined: the two constraints describe the same line.

\par

\par\medskip


\subsubsection{Question 3}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:question-3}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:lec04-tldr-q3}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original practice question}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
A noisy matrix has singular values \((4,2,0.2)\). What singular values do rank\sphinxhyphen{}two F correction and essential\sphinxhyphen{}form correction use?

\par\medskip

\par\medskip
\textbf{Worked solution}\par\smallskip

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Apply the rank\sphinxhyphen{}two F rule}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Only the smallest singular value must be zero.
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\Sigma_F=\begin{pmatrix}4&0&0\\0&2&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Apply the essential\sphinxhyphen{}matrix rule}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The first two singular values must also agree.
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
a=(4+2)/2=3,\qquad\Sigma_E=\begin{pmatrix}3&0&0\\0&3&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus F uses {\color{QuizMathBlue} \((4,2,0)\)} and E uses {\color{QuizMathBlue} \((3,3,0)\)}.

\par

\par\medskip


\subsubsection{Question 4}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:question-4}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:lec04-tldr-q4}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original practice question}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
A candidate pose reconstructs a point with depths \(+5\) and \(-5\) in the two cameras. Is that point a valid visible correspondence under that pose?

\par\medskip

\par\medskip
\textbf{Worked solution}\par\smallskip

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Check the first camera}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} A visible point must have positive camera\sphinxhyphen{}frame depth.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first depth {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(+5>0\)} passes the first camera’s test.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Check the second camera}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Cheirality requires positive depth in both observing cameras.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The second depth {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(-5<0\)} fails. Reject this point/pose combination as a valid visible correspondence.

\par

\par\medskip


\subsubsection{Question 5}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:question-5}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:lec04-tldr-q5}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original practice question}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
Rectified cameras have \(b=0.2\,\mathrm m\), \(f=600\) pixels, \(d=30\) pixels. What is the depth? If measured disparity becomes 31, is the point reconstructed nearer or farther?

\par\medskip

\par\medskip
\textbf{Worked solution}\par\smallskip

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Compute the true depth}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Baseline and depth both use meters; focal length and disparity both use pixels.
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
fb=600(0.2)=120\,\mathrm{m\,px},\qquad Z=120/30=4\,\mathrm m.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Compute the perturbed depth and sign}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} A larger disparity should place the estimate nearer.
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\widehat Z=\frac{120}{31}\,\mathrm m,\qquad\Delta Z=\frac{120}{31}-4=\frac{120-124}{31}=-\frac4{31}\,\mathrm m\approx-0.1290\,\mathrm m.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The estimate is nearer.

\par

\par\medskip


\subsubsection{Question 6}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:question-6}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:lec04-tldr-q6}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original practice question}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
For that setup, which disparity interval corresponds to depths from 2 to 6 meters?

\par\medskip

\par\medskip
\textbf{Worked solution}\par\smallskip

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Evaluate the far limit}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Inverse depth makes the far endpoint the smaller disparity.
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
d_{min}=\frac{fb}{Z_{max}}=\frac{120}{6}=20\,\mathrm{pixels}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Evaluate the near limit}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The closer endpoint has the larger disparity.
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
d_{max}=\frac{120}{2}=60\,\mathrm{pixels},\qquad d\in[20,60].
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip


\subsubsection{Question 7}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:question-7}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:lec04-tldr-q7}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original practice question}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
Which direction do you optimize SAD and NCC? Can a constant\sphinxhyphen{}intensity patch supply a defined zero\sphinxhyphen{}mean NCC score?

\par\medskip

\par\medskip
\textbf{Worked solution}\par\smallskip

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Identify what each score rewards}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Difference costs reward small disagreement; correlation rewards similar centered patterns.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Minimize SAD. Maximize zero\sphinxhyphen{}mean NCC, or equivalently minimize a consistently defined negative correlation cost.

\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Check the NCC denominator}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} A flat patch has no centered contrast to normalize.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For constant {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(I_i=c\)}, every {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(I_i-\bar I=0\)}, so {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(\sqrt{\sum_i(I_i-\bar I)^2}=0\)}. The NCC denominator vanishes; the normalized score is undefined.

\par

\par\medskip


\subsubsection{Question 8}
\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:question-8}}\label{\detokenize{lectures/lecture04/tldr:lec04-tldr-q8}}
\par\medskip\textbf{Original practice question}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
With center intensity 10 and ordered neighbors \((8,12,7,11)\), what are the Census string and rank under the strict darker\sphinxhyphen{}than\sphinxhyphen{}center convention?

\par\medskip

\par\medskip
\textbf{Worked solution}\par\smallskip

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 1 — Compare each neighbor with the center}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} The strict darker\sphinxhyphen{}than\sphinxhyphen{}center convention assigns one to values below 10.
{\color{QuizMathBlue} \begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\begin{pmatrix}8<10\\12<10\\7<10\\11<10\end{pmatrix}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}}
\par

\par\medskip\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
{\color{QuizStepRed}\bfseries Step 2 — Read the string and count its ones}\par\smallskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why:} Census retains order; rank retains only the count.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Census string is {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(1010\)}. The rank is {\color{QuizMathBlue} \(1+0+1+0=2\)}.

\par

\par\medskip
